London has found another way to spend a fiver standing up.

The pizza slice, once principally the food of New Yorkers, students and anyone making questionable decisions after midnight, is having a rather polished moment. Across the capital, enormous triangular wedges are appearing for £4, £5, sometimes £6 or more, topped with everything from pepperoni and hot honey to burrata and vodka sauce. You can fold them. You can walk with them. You can take nice photos of them.

At Carmy’s, a new New York-style slice shop that opened in Covent Garden this summer, a cheese slice is £4.25. At Voodoo Ray’s in Dalston, which has been doing this since 2012, a margherita is £4.90 and pepperoni £5.40. Paulie’s in Shoreditch starts at £5 for its classic NYC and runs to £6.50 for burrata or cacio e pepe. Homeslice, which opened in 2013, starts at £5.50.

open image in gallery Big smoke slices: Parlours serving up individual triangles have cropped up all over London and beyond ( Getty/iStock )

It is spreading. Dough Hands, already one of London’s more talked-about pizza operations, started selling individual slices from its 20-inch pies for the first time at All My Friends in Hackney Wick this year. Further north, Edinburgh’s Civerinos now has three dedicated slice bars, with prices for New York-style slices ranging from £4-6.

Five or six quid for one slice of pizza can, nonetheless, induce the sort of reaction normally reserved for captive audiences in airport Prets. Phil Chaykin, one of the five owners of Carmy’s, knows this because people told him. “When we first opened, there were quite a few comments online saying that £4+ for a slice of pizza was expensive,” he tells me. “I think part of that is simply because people aren’t yet used to judging pizza by the slice.”

There is a catch. The slice is admittedly enormous.

open image in gallery Saucy and scenic: many sliced pizza parlours lack seating – but customers are happy to chow down standing up ( Getty/iStock )

Carmy’s pizzas are 20 inches across and cut into eight. A 20-inch pizza has nearly three times the surface area of a 12-inch one, meaning its £4.25 cheese slice works out at roughly the same amount of pizza for your money as a £12 12-inch pizza.

“Our slices are substantial – two are enough for an average person to be full, and a whole 20-inch pizza is really something to share between three or four people,” Chaykin says. “You can get a lunch for less than £10 per person – is that really that expensive for central London?”

Pizza geometry is unlikely to be something any of us care to revisit after GCSE maths, but it is helpful here. We hear “one slice” and picture one eighth of a normal pizza. These things are closer to individual meals. Voodoo Ray’s goes bigger, at 22 inches. Each of those is cut into eight giant slices. Its £29.50 margherita would bring in £39.20 if all eight pieces were sold separately at £4.90. Its £35 pepperoni becomes £43.20 at £5.40 a slice.

open image in gallery Taking a cut: the maths of the slice can be more generous than it first appears ( Getty/iStock )

At which point one might reasonably conclude that pizza is an exceptionally good business to be in. Flour and water are cheap. Tomato is not caviar. Cut the thing up and somehow another tenner appears.

If only restaurants worked like that.

Carmy’s aims for an upper limit of roughly 25 per cent food cost across its menu, Chaykin says. Even using good flour, San Marzano tomatoes, quality cheese and carefully sourced produce, pizza’s raw ingredients remain relatively inexpensive.

Our dough takes a minimum of 72 hours from start to finish, and there are no shortcuts in that process Phil Chaykin, co-owner of Carmy’s

The expensive part is persuading those ingredients to become pizza.

“Our dough takes a minimum of 72 hours from start to finish, and there are no shortcuts in that process,” he says. “Making the dough, balling it, managing fermentation, stretching, topping, baking and then reheating slices to order all require skilled labour.” In fact, he says selling whole pizzas is easier. Slices create more potential waste and require another step: a defining feature of the New York slice is its final blast in the oven, crisping the base immediately before it reaches your hand.

“So while a slice shop might look like a simpler or cheaper operation than a sit-down pizzeria, the economics aren’t dramatically different,” Chaykin says. “Ultimately, our pricing has to support a very labour-intensive product as well as the quality of ingredients we’re using.”

open image in gallery A few pounds and a paper plate, and lunch is sorted ( Getty/iStock )

A £5 hot takeaway slice also contains about 83p in VAT before anybody has been paid or the lights switched on. Rent, rates, energy, equipment, insurance and card fees are all still waiting patiently for their portion.

There are easier moments to own a restaurant. The UK’s 100 largest restaurant groups saw combined profits fall 44 per cent in the most recent year, even as their revenues rose. It is quite possible, apparently, to sell more food and reap fewer rewards.

The real advantage of the slice reveals itself when you look around Carmy’s. There are no reservations, no table service and only limited seating. Most customers arrive, buy pizza and leave. “The physical model is definitely important,” Chaykin says. “We can serve a lot of people from a relatively small space, and because there are no reservations or traditional table service, customers can be in and out very quickly.

“At busy times we can serve a very large number of customers in a short period without needing a corresponding number of seats. That’s really what makes a small space work for us.”

The appeal on the other side of the counter is considerably less complicated. “The great thing about the format is that it serves quite different occasions,” Chaykin says. “Someone might come in on their own, grab one slice and eat it on the go. Someone else might have two slices and a drink, while a couple with two children might take a whole pie and share it.”

It also happens to fit rather neatly with the way London eats now. “Everyone is busy, people increasingly want something genuinely good without necessarily committing to a full restaurant meal, and a slice is probably the ultimate grab-and-go food.”

Waste, which ought to be the model’s obvious weakness, has so far proved less troublesome than expected at Carmy’s. Production is adjusted throughout the day to avoid leaving slices sitting around and staff take home much of what remains at closing time.

“In practice, the bigger commercial risk for us has been the opposite: not having enough pizza ready when demand suddenly picks up,” Chaykin says. “We’re much more likely to lose revenue because customers are waiting for the next pizza to come out of the oven than because we’ve made too much.”

open image in gallery New York-style pizza has become the slice to be seen with ( Getty/iStock )

None of this was invented in Covent Garden. Pizza spent its early life in Naples as inexpensive food that could be eaten in the street; Italian migrants carried it across the Atlantic and New York turned giant, foldable slices into a civic institution. “In New York, slice culture is an iconic part of daily life,” Chaykin says. “It’s affordable, grab-and-go, the menus are usually simple, and the shops themselves can be very basic. New York is also one of America’s great walking cities, so the slice naturally became part of its street-food culture.”

The capital, he argues, ought to have been fertile ground all along. “London is arguably even more suited to that way of eating. We walk everywhere, we use public transport, we eat on the move – so I’ve always found it slightly surprising that we never developed the same kind of slice culture here.”

London has sold pizza by the slice for years, but Chaykin thinks something about it has changed: “the pizza itself.”

“New York has seen a new generation of pizza makers applying almost a high-end bakery mentality to the slice shop – much more attention to flour, fermentation and dough-making, combined with a chef-led approach to ingredients and toppings,” he says

The modern slice has managed to become fast food with a 72-hour dough, cheap lunch with expensive cheese, a bit of New York theatre and something you can eat alone over a bin without feeling you have made a poor life choice. London has practically run with the idea.

For the people selling it, cheap flour helps. More important is being able to serve a lot of people with not very much room. For everyone else, the calculation is simpler. You have a fiver. There is a very large piece of pizza in front of you. Good luck walking past.

News.title: Inside the reality of Man United’s budget rebuild – and the question it asks of Michael Carrick
News.content:

There is a table Manchester United top during Michael Carrick’s reign and it is the one that matters most. No one has taken more points since his January appointment. Over the last 13 years, however, United have been more accustomed to topping the spending charts. Now they may have a different kind of mid-table mediocrity, at least for those with an obsession with the transfer window.

When it closed, United were in the bottom half, according to Transfermarkt figures: there was an outlay of £148m, potentially rising to £155m, on midfielders, but no other purchase of a senior player. In contrast, Manchester City spent more than £400m, Chelsea and Tottenham over £300m, Newcastle, Aston Villa, Liverpool and Arsenal over £200m. Down in 11th place, United were outspent by promoted Ipswich and Hull.

Is this austerity, Old Trafford style? Carrick is not one to criticise his club. He stressed he is happy with the signings they have made; without the extra left-back that, by common consensus, they required, or another striker that many would have wanted, is the issue the signings they have not made? Carrick hinted as much.

open image in gallery Michael Carrick claims to be ‘largely’ happy with Manchester United's summer transfer business despite being outspent by rivals and seemingly left short in some areas ( PA )

“Certainly, the players that we've brought into the group, I'm absolutely delighted with,” he said. “I think we've done some really good business there for the quality and the level of player that we've got. You can always look at it, and there's other things you can do or possibly could have done.”

There was the sense that United could not have done them; not in terms of high-grade targets, anyway. They were offered Rayan Ait-Nouri on loan on deadline day. They surely could not have bought Lewis Hall this summer, even if Newcastle were willing to sell.

Perhaps a host of factors coalesced. One was a regular reason: United’s inability to sell the unwanted. It was scarcely their fault that Manuel Ugarte was injured at the World Cup but they may have started the summer envisaging bringing in fees for the Uruguayan, Andre Onana and Joshua Zirkzee. Instead, the forward remains at Old Trafford and the goalkeeper has been loaned back to Trabzonspor. They may come to be grateful that Barcelona did not take up their option to buy Marcus Rashford: a proposed fee of £26m may come to look absurdly cheap and the Mancunian, unlike the others, has the quality to become a first choice.

But whereas United may have imagined bringing in an extra £50m, and perhaps even £100m, the only significant sum they banked came courtesy of a deal for Rasmus Hojlund with Napoli that was arranged in 2025. Remove that and only Coventry earned less money from sales than United. They occupy a higher place in the net-spend charts – Villa and Chelsea made profits while, for much of the summer, Newcastle were on course to – and seem an anomaly compared to the clubs who trade constantly.

They could look an anachronism in other respects, too: the inflation in transfer-market fees may be ridiculous but it appeared to catch United out. Midfielders they admired, whether Elliot Anderson or Mateus Fernandes, started to go for colossal fees. United could not compete.

But if United have their own credit crunch, it also reflects on past spending. The big losses they made on players such as Antony and Casemiro may have caught up with them. Even as Senne Lammens was a bargain last summer, there is a question if they paid over the odds for at least some of the £200m attacking trio of Bryan Mbeumo, Mateus Cunha and Benjamin Sesko. Their annual accounts invariably show the millions they owe other clubs in transfer fees. Plus, of course, there is the annual interest payments to service the debt the Glazers landed on the club.

open image in gallery United’s spending suggests they are upgrading their first team one department at a time ( AFP/Getty )

And Ruben Amorim’s reign cost United, whether in the €11m compensation Sporting CP received, or carrying on paying the Portuguese after his sacking. Finishing 15th in the Premier League in 2025 meant far less prize money; playing only 40 games last season – their Carabao Cup exit to Grimsby was under Amorim, the FA Cup defeat to Brighton under Darren Fletcher – also reduced their income.

So United’s has been something of a budget rebuild. Youri Tielemans’ £35m release clause meant he was £90m less than Enzo Fernandez. Andrey Santos was £77m cheaper than his former Chelsea teammate, even if he was often on the bench at Stamford Bridge while the Argentinian was in the team. At an initial £65m, Carlos Baleba was the most expensive of the trio but still only the 10th biggest buy by a Premier League club this summer.

“For what we've spent, we've certainly made the most of it, without a shadow of a doubt,” said Carrick. But maybe the most instructive element is what United have spent, how it compares and whether it leaves them short. There is a wider sense that no one has got everything they wanted. “What squad's ever the perfect squad?” mused Carrick. “You've always got to find ways of adapting.” Maybe United’s lack of spending power will put more onus on him to adapt.

Donald Trump has claimed the US has “an idea for peace” as he sends his special envoy Steve Witkoff for talks with both Moscow and Kyiv.

Speaking to press on Friday, the president suggested the US had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, which is now in its fifth year. He did not, however, elaborate on what that proposal would be.

Nor did he say if ⁠Witkoff or his son-in-law Jared Kushner would be traveling to ​Ukraine, ⁠Russia or both nations.

It comes after reports that Witkoff is “too scared” to travel to Kyiv for peace talks throwing planned negotiations into doubt.

The Kyiv visit was thrown into doubt amid claims that Witkoff is concerned about Russian warnings that he should not travel to the Ukrainian capital, the Kyiv Independent reported.

"The Russians don't want them to come here to Kyiv, and Witkoff is always sensitive to Russian sentiment,” a source told the outlet. "They're being told there that it's dangerous."

The pair were due to arrive in Kyiv by plane, with the outlet previously reporting that Witkoff does not like taking the train to Kyiv.

Kenya's president William Ruto on Friday directed Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the Indian company failed to generate any economic impact in one of Kenya's most important export sectors.

Tata Chemicals produces soda ash from Lake Magadi that is used in the manufacture of glass, soaps and detergents. Kenya's exports of soda ash came to 254,779 tons, valued at $56.9m, in the year to July 2025, according to government data.

The company should “pack and leave” in place of a new investor, Mr Ruto said at a public rally on Thursday.

( Reuters )

Tata Chemicals Magadi Limited has been in Kenya since 2005. Its operations were suspended by Kenya's ministry of mining in July, pending a “compliance review."

The company’s departure from Kenya could lead to job losses and significant loss of revenue.

Mr Ruto said while soda ash from Lake Magadi is capable of changing Kenya for the better, the Indian company has “not built anything in Kajiado", the county where the lake is located.

“They have not built any factory or employed people,” he said.

“I told them to pack and leave. They have been taking our resources and shipping them to India. We will bring a new company and the condition set is they must build a glass factory here," the Kenyan leader added.

Tata Chemicals Magadi Limited said in a communication to the National Stock Exchange of India on Friday that it is “fully compliant” in Kenya and is awaiting communication from the Kenyan government regarding a review of its operations.

The company did not say whether it had officially received orders to leave Kenya, but added said it remains “committed to constructive engagement.”

Soda ash is produced from trona, a naturally occurring sodium carbonate mineral extracted from Lake Magadi. Large scale commercial production of soda ash in the area started in 1911.

Pretty much everyone on stage at the Metropolitan Opera in New York must audition — even the snake who will briefly take center stage in an upcoming adaptation of a Mozart classic.

In charge of deciding who gets the s-s-s-s-starring reptilian role is Zoe Ziegfeld, a carnival performer-turned-opera actor cast as the snake handler in the Met's version of “Così fan tutte," inspired by Coney Island in the 1950s.

Ziegfeld takes each snake, lets it slither and wrap around, then hoists the animal over their head, rehearsing what they will do under the bright lights at center stage for each performance. Ziegfeld looks each one in the eye, almost face-to-face as they evaluate the snake's demeanor.

“I need to know that the animal is comfortable with people and with what we are doing,” Ziegfeld said.

Princess slithers into her big role

In the cold-blooded competition, a boa constrictor named Princess won. She is a larger snake with a better visual presence on stage.

“We will be moving forward with Princess (the big sun-glow boa constrictor who is yellow-peach) in rehearsals on a trial basis! She is a wonderful snake, and the trial is not about her, but rather about me and my strength," Ziegfeld wrote in an email after the auditions were over.

A slightly smaller brown boa constrictor named Nala from a second audition will be Princess' understudy.

A Mozart opera set at a 1950s Coney Island carnival

This is the third time Ziegfeld has played the role of the snake charmer in the Met's adaptation of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's 1790 opera.

In Mozart’s original, two Italian soldiers decide to test their lovers’ fidelity by pretending to head off to war. They then disguise themselves and try to seduce each other’s girlfriends. In this version, the plot remains mostly the same, but the setting is a 1950s Coney Island carnival complete with vibrant scenery and sideshow performers.

Carnaval snake charmer turned opera performer

Ziegfeld came to the role honestly. They spent a couple of seasons on Coney Island doing eight snake-charming shows a day.

When they tried out several years ago, live snakes weren’t allowed in the audition space. So instead, Ziegfeld brought video of their snake-charming act, then hammered home their carnival sideshow bona fides by knocking a nail into their own nasal cavity in what was called the Human Blockhead act.

“The music’s different. The money is different. It’s a pleasure to entertain. And with snakes, it’s a delight to know that there are people watching who are in awe and people who are terrified. And those things happen at the Met and at Coney — so I would say they are more alike than different, to be honest,” Ziegfeld said.

Animals are important characters at some Met operas

The snakes came to their audition thanks to Nancy Novograd and her company All Tame Animals.

She got into the business when her horse appeared onstage at the Met in a production of “Carmen,” and now she provides the opera house with everything from elephants to insects.

The first two snakes to audition were a bit small. One might have clashed with Ziegfeld's top. But the key is personality, Novograd said.

“Animals have to perform as do human talent. Sometimes they have a set type of behaviors that they have to demonstrate. And sometimes they just have to get along with the talent," Novograd said. “So in this case, they have to be the right color, size, and Zoe has to like them.”

___

Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

Four people were killed and two were critically injured in an auto wreck when a car veered off a mountain road near Wrightwood, California, early on Friday.

"For unknown reasons, the vehicle swerved away from the roadway, struck a telephone pole and rolled down an embankment. At that time, four parties were ejected from the vehicle," California Highway Patrol Officer Thaniel Ong told ABC 7.

The crash, which was called in around 1:30am, occurred on Highway 2, between Big Pines and Wrightwood, near the LA-San Bernardino County line.

Most of those inside the 2016 Hyundai Veloster were not wearing seat belts and alcohol is thought to be a contributing factor to the crash, according to officials.

According to CHP, all six people involved in the crash are from Wrightwood, a town of about 5,000 people in the mountains north of Los Angeles.

Four people were killed and two were seriously injured in a rollover crash in the mountains north of Los Angeles early Friday morning ( ABC7 screengrab )

The dead include two women and two men.

Responding to the scene involved a complicated rescue process because most of the occupants were scattered outside the car and responders didn’t know how many people had been inside, Chris Prater, a public information officer for the San Bernardino County Fire Department, told The Los Angeles Times.

Upon searching the scene, responders found five people had been ejected from the car, and a sixth person, who had been wearing a seat belt, took it off and exited the vehicle.

Four people were confirmed dead on the scene, while two were flown by air ambulances to Arrowhead Regional Medical Center in Colton in critical condition.

“The CHP reminds all motorists and passengers that seat belts save lives,” the agency told the paper. “Wearing a seat belt is the single most effective action a person can take to protect themselves in the event of a traffic collision.”

“Impaired driving is illegal, dangerous, and entirely preventable,” the statement added. “If you plan to consume alcohol, designate a sober driver, use a rideshare service, or contact a friend or family member.”

News.content:

The closely watched case of the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children was on the verge of being declared a mistrial Friday — but there was still one more dramatic moment to come.

After weeks of grueling testimony, the jury could not get beyond an impasse on the seventh day of deliberations on murder charges against Lindsay Clancy. An audible gasp was heard in the courtroom as Judge William F. Sullivan said he was going to to end their deliberations without reaching a verdict.

But just as the jurors were about to come back to the courtroom, Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer asked to make a last-minute request for a higher court to stave off the mistrial. That kicked off a tense wait while a judge on the state’s top court considered the ask.

The whiplash moment was one last piece of courtroom drama in a livestreamed trial that captivated and divided many across the nation. And now prosecutors must decide whether to do it all over again with a second trial.

Ultimately on Friday, the high court denied the defense attorney's appeal and the judge formally declared a mistrial later in the afternoon. Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, blamed a lone juror for the impasse. Defense attorneys argued in their written petition that the person had revealed a possible bias against those dealing with mental illness.

Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, never disputed that she killed her children, but her attorney said she was experiencing a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids, the youngest just 8 months old, and then tried to take her own life in 2023. Prosecutors said Clancy knew what she was doing and should be held criminally responsible.

The jury foreperson had previously told Sullivan that a single juror wouldn’t follow the court’s instruction about reasonable doubt, according to Reddington.

In their last-minute appeal, Clancy’s lawyers had argued the juror should, at minimum, be questioned more thoroughly by the judge, or even dismissed outright before a mistrial was declared. Prosecutors responded that there was nothing in the jury’s notes indicating the juror in question had “a lack of impartiality, bias, extraneous influence, or inability to deliberate.”

Jurors had heard competing expert testimony about Clancy’s mental health.

Massachusetts defense attorney Joseph Perullo, who was not involved in the case, said it was “clear cut” for him, but he acknowledged that jurors could have difficulties.

“It’s clear that Lindsay had a psychotic break, and the psychotic break led her to kill her children,” he said. “But the prosecution can tell you that she sent her husband off for errands and therefore she is criminally responsible.”

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said after the mistrial was declared there would not be an immediate decision on whether to go forward with a second trial.

Perullo said he is hopeful prosecutors will speak to Patrick Clancy, the children's father, and other family.

“It is a tremendous stress on them to do it again, and it's going to be an even bigger circus,” he said.

But Crystal Lyons, a former prosecutor in Massachusetts, believes prosecutors don't have the option not to retry Lindsay Clancy.

“At the end of the day, it was a tragedy where there were three young children who lost their lives,” she said.

News.title: Alexander Isak finally starts to justify £125m price tag with fine double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

News.title: When is Black Friday 2026? This year’s dates and what to expect
News.content:
Five tips for finding genuine Black Friday discounts and deals

Learning how to find the best Black Friday discounts can make a meaningful difference to your festive budget, especially if you’re a keen sale shopper. The following five tips are a good starting point.

1. Don’t over-fixate on Black Friday itself

Although the day of Black Friday brings some of the best discounts of the festive sale season, good deals are likely to be available both before and after it – and some items may sell out.

“When we look at our pricing data on a daily level, you have certain events such as Amazon’s October Prime sale [not yet confirmed for 2026] that are an earlier vector for change in prices,” says Vivek Pandya, a director at Adobe for Business.

“We typically see more significant discounts starting to emerge as we get into late October or early November, and these really kick up a notch as we get into Black Friday week.”

So, while interest in Black Friday deals will peak around the day itself, some of the best deals may have been available since the beginning of the week, or earlier.

2. Expand your search to everyday essentials

At Telegraph Recommended, we’ve picked up on a proliferation of discounts on everyday household items during recent Black Friday sales (and during other occasional events such as Prime Day). If you need a top-up of items such as cleaning products or pet supplies, this could be a thrifty time to buy them.

“These sales have become a spending spree on what retailers frame as ‘everyday essentials’, as well as bigger items and gifts,” says Pandya. Last year’s Cyber Weekend saw a 260 per cent spike in sales of “personal care” items including cosmetics, shampoos, fragrances and toothbrushes, according to Adobe.

3. Use a price tracker

Free price tracking tools such as camelcamelcamel can show you how the price of a product has changed over time. This allows you to identify when a Black Friday deal has actually brought a product’s price significantly lower than usual, or when the retailer’s pricing strategy has artificially made a deal appear to be generous.

Gabrielė Vitkė, product marketing team lead at data-gathering specialist Decodo, warns shoppers to watch out for “anchoring”, where a product’s price is set high prior to Black Friday, allowing the retailer then to reduce it sharply and advertise an eye-catching reduction.

“Discounts on items such as electronics and computing products can seem steep, sometimes exceeding 50 per cent against the list price,” says Vitkė. “However, our data shows that prices in this category rose in the run-up to Black Friday 2025, which is a sign of anchor pricing before the ‘discount’ is applied.”

News.title: Indonesia wildfires trigger 50,000 respiratory infections
News.content:
More than 50,000 people have contracted respiratory infections in Indonesia, as raging wild fires blanket huge swathes of the country in a thick, toxic smoke.

The vast archipelago is only a month into its fire season, but intense blazes have proven hard to control across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo. There are fears the situation will only get worse, because the “Godzilla” El Niño is set to suppress rains that would normally have helped extinguish the flames.

“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño,” said Raja Juli Antoni, the forestry minister. “September is the main fight for us.”

Already the toxic haze has spread across Southeast Asia. On Friday Kuching, a city in Malaysian Borneo, was the most polluted city in the world on the IQ Air Index, followed by Jakarta and Singapore.

The wildfires have brought memories of record-breaking blazes in 2015. Then, the smoke was linked to roughly 100,000 excess deaths in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, according to one study. The World Bank said Indonesia alone saw economic losses of $16.1bn, or 2 per cent of GDP.

News.title: Global hunger is a threat to Britain’s national security, report says
News.content:
Global hunger poses a direct threat to Britain’s national security, and tackling it should be a government priority, a new report from the London School of Economics has warned.

It says hunger is a major driver of mass migration, extreme violence and war – events that threaten significant repercussions for Britain and Europe’s national security.

“Hunger prevention is an important part of national security policy, not an optional act of charity,” Stuart Gordon, professor of International Development at LSE and author of the report, told The Telegraph.

Recent hunger crises in places like Sudan, Afghanistan and across North Africa have contributed significantly to rising numbers of people moving to the West.

Between January and November 2025 alone, 12,684 migrants from Sudan – which is facing what has been described as the worst hunger crisis in Africa’s history – arrived in Europe, roughly three times as many as the previous year.

Last year, an estimated 155,000 African refugees arrived in Europe.

“Food insecurity tests one of the most basic expectations people have of government: that it will protect access to the essentials of life,” said Prof Gordon.

“Food price shocks can rapidly escalate into political instability when governments are perceived to have failed to protect access to basic subsistence goods,” he added.

News.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak slows at epicentre but widens elsewhere, modelling suggests
News.content:
Congo’s Ebola outbreak shows signs of slowing at the epicentre of the flare-up, but is widening as the infection spreads further afield, modelling suggests.

The daily tally of new cases in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was falling at the end of August, but more cases were being found outside Ituri province, where the infection burst out.

Latest official figures say the outbreak has now killed more than 3,000 people out of over 6,100 confirmed cases, with the infection spreading faster than any previous epidemic of the viral haemorrhagic fever.

Modelling by Airfinity, a health analytics firm, suggests the true toll of cases could be more than four times higher than reported.

The outbreak remains on track to eclipse the 2014 West Africa outbreak later this month, to become the largest ever recorded.

Airfinity said that data from late August showed the seven-day averages of reported cases and reported deaths had fallen by 16 per cent and 18 per cent respectively.

The firm said it was “too early to confirm the decline will hold, and it may mask subnational variation: The outbreak has fluctuated before and a week of falling case and death counts does not rule out another surge.

“Even if the decline continues at this current pace, low case levels remain weeks away.”

News.title: Bank of England must raise interest rates, says chief economist
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Government borrowing costs edged lower on Thursday as Andy Burnham continues to face scrutiny over the public finances.

The yield on 10-year US treasury bonds – considered a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money – declined slightly to 4.78pc on Thursday after a drop in oil prices.

Pre-market trading of bonds in Britain, France and Germany suggested the market was poised to rally after a brutal first half of the week.

However, Mr Burnham and Chancellor John Healey remain under intense pressure, with analysts estimating that as much as half of the country’s fiscal headroom has been wiped out by the jump in bond yields.

Borrowing costs surged after a jump in oil prices caused by fresh strikes between the US and Iran.

The yield on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, hit levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2007, while longer-term debt costs hit their highest point since 1998.

It means the Chancellor will have less room for manoeuvre in the Budget next month, with some economists predicting the rise in borrowing costs has wiped out up to £14bn of breathing room.

The rise in bond yields across major economies had deepened concerns about deteriorating financial conditions.

Central banks in the US and Europe are increasingly expected to raise interest rates this month to combat inflation caused by the Iran war, although the Bank of England is expected to hold rates steady for now.

Gavin Friend, an analyst at NAB, said: “If this war ‌were to be ‌put to bed, then that ⁠would certainly be something very positive to bring yields back down again across the board.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Oil prices slipped, helping boost stocks and bonds.

Renewed fighting between the US and Iran pushed oil prices sharply higher earlier in the week.

However, Brent crude was trading near $94 a barrel after Donald Trump said he does not expect the US bombing campaign to last “much longer”.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 advanced 0.2pc to 64,455.83. Among major gainers, OpenAI investor SoftBank Group rose 2.9pc, memory chipmaker Kioxia rose 0.6pc, and chip equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron gained 0.8pc.

South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.4pc to 6,656.81. Samsung was 1.3pc higher, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix was up 1.4pc.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng edged 0.1pc higher, to 25,344.80. The Shanghai Composite index climbed 0.4pc to 3,958.79.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5pc to 9,025.10.

The Taiex in Taiwan rose 0.6pc, while India’s Sensex climbed 0.3pc.

It comes after Wall Street bounced back after its sharp sell-off at the start of September, as investors snapped up shares that had fallen in recent days.

The S&P 500 rose, with almost 350 companies ending higher. Dell was among the biggest winners, jumping 14pc after giving an upbeat outlook, while investors were also looking ahead to results from chipmaker Broadcom.

The recovery came despite continued concerns over inflation, with oil prices remaining high as fighting between the US and Iran escalated. Brent crude briefly climbed close to $97 a barrel before easing back after Donald Trump said he did not expect the renewed bombing campaign to last “too long”.

US government bond yields were little changed after surging to their highest levels in several years earlier in the week.

Investors also got a mixed picture from the Federal Reserve’s latest assessment of the US economy. Economic activity increased modestly over the past two months, helped by strong demand from data centres, while companies added jobs at a slower pace in August.

The figures come ahead of Friday’s closely watched US jobs report, which could influence expectations for the next move in interest rates.

News.title: Weapons and mercenaries from foreign states fuelling Sudan’s war, UN report finds
News.content:
The war in Sudan is being fuelled by weapons and mercenaries from external states including the United Arab Emirates, Colombia and Turkey, a United Nations report has found.

An investigation by a UN fact-finding mission published on Thursday found that the supply of drones in particular to both sides in the civil war was extending the fighting’s reach and contributing to war crimes.

“Increasingly sophisticated drone capabilities [has] enabled both parties to strike far beyond immediate front lines”, says the report.

“The [UN] mission calls on States to enforce the Darfur arms embargo and suspend transfers of weapons, drones, components, or military assistance where there is a substantial risk of their use in serious violations”.

Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the head of the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Hundreds of thousands have died and some 14 million people have been displaced in what has become the world’s deadliest conflict.

In a previous report in February, following the capture of El Fasher in which at least 60,000 people were killed, the UN said the RSF’s mass killings of Black African ethnic groups, including Zaghawa and Fur, bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.

The latest report said “individuals and entities” in the UAE were part of a transnational network supplying weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel to the RSF – including NORINCO AH-4 howitzers, FK-20000 air defence systems and Chinese-made CH-95 strike drones.

The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), meanwhile, separately obtained Turkish-manufactured drones, including Bayraktar Akıncı combat drones and Yiha III loitering munitions.

The Turkish embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

Sports.title: Fraudster who pawned Edgar Davids’ £188,000 art collection misses sentencing after ‘being knocked out by luggage’
Sports.content:
NO SHOW Fraudster who pawned Edgar Davids’ £188,000 art collection misses sentencing after ‘being knocked out by luggage’

A FRAUDSTER who pawned Edgar Davids’ £188,000 art collection has claimed she failed to appear in court because she was knocked out by luggage.

The football legend, 52, allowed friend Nabila Habiby to stay at his Hadley Wood mansion in 2014.



Davids believed that Habiby was looking after his possessions while he moved into a new Central London flat in December of that year.

But a court has since heard that Habiby, 39, stole 37 pieces of art across the following two years before taking them to pawn brokers, with Davids believing that they were being stored at a unit in Enfield.



Habiby managed to obtain £31,500 in loans by handing over the 37 painting and works of art belonging to Davids.

The former Spurs and Ajax midfielder only realised his paintings had gone when Habiby defaulted on the loans.

A court heard that the pawn shops sold the art to collectors around the world with one getting in touch with him to inquire about the history of a painting.

Habiby pleaded guilty in September 2025 to two counts of fraud, and she was set free on bail with a warning that she could face up to 34 months in prison.

She has still not been sentenced, with the first attempt derailing after she made a failed attempt to withdraw her guilty pleas.

Her case was listed for sentence again today, but Habiby was absent from the dock at Wood Green Crown Court.



Defence barrister Hannah Thomas said: “I received correspondence this morning, at around 9.30am, saying on her way to the airport to come here she had been hit on the head by a piece of luggage en route.

“She had a concussion, since she passed out, and was taken to the hospital where she remains on a drip.”

Judge Emma Deacon KC said she had been handed “inadequate” medical evidence from Belgium – where Habiby now lives – to support her story, however.

The judge did agree to adjourn the sentencing hearing though, so that the original judge who oversaw the case when guilty pleas were entered could pass sentence.

It is now almost five years since Habiby was first charged after a Metropolitan Police investigation.



Her fraud offences date back to 2015 and 2016.

The court heard the former baller handed Habiby, a wealth manager, the keys to his home in Hadley Wood, Hertfordshire, when he was moving to an apartment in central London in December 2014.

She took his collection of works by artists Paul Insect and Ron English, which he had bought from the Opera Gallery in New York between 2006 and 2012, to pawnbrokers.

Some of the paintings have since been recovered, but 25 works of art are gone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Habiby has been ordered to come to court on September 23 to be sentenced.



She has also been told to provide a full medical report to back up her absence from court on Friday.

Sports.title: Troy Parrott comes back to haunt Jose Mourinho as ex-Tottenham star comes off bench to score winner vs Real Madrid
Sports.content:
TROY PARROTT came back to haunt Jose Mourinho as he condemned him to his first defeat as Real Madrid manager.

The Ireland ace came off the bench to score an 81st-minute winner for Real Betis against the Spanish giants.

Mourinho had overseen a 100 per cent winning start to the season as Madrid kept pace with hated rivals Barcelona.



However, the first slip-up of the campaign came on Friday night against Betis as Parrott was quickest to react to a loose ball following a Thibaut Courtois save at a corner, and smashed home the winner into the roof of the net.



But Mourinho, 63, might have guessed such an event might happen given he handed Parrott his debut when he was manager of Tottenham.

Mourinho famously gave Parrott the match ball after his Premier League debut off the bench, a 5-0 win for Tottenham in 2019.

A missed Kylian Mbappe penalty then added salt to the wounds for an awful evening for Los Blancos, as Parrott became only the second Irishman to score against Real Madrid after John Aldridge’s goals for Real Sociedad in 1989-90 and 1990-91.



On the winning goal, Parrott – in comments which would certainly please compatriot Roy Keane – told ESPN: “That’s a striker’s job, to go in after the ball and hope it will fall in front of me.

“In a game I might do this 10 times and it might not happen.

“So it’s a mentality thing to just keep going in there and hopefully it comes, and today it did.”

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK



Parrott would go on to have loans at Millwall, Ipswich, MK Dons, Preston North End and Excelsior before leaving Spurs permanently in 2024.

He joined Dutch side AZ, scoring 51 goals in 97 games before signing for Betis in a £17.1million (€20m) deal this summer.

Parrott’s match-winning goal, on his home debut no less, moved Betis level with Madrid on points and into the top three of La Liga before the rest of the league play their games this weekend.

Mourinho had a few sour grapes about the result, however, saying: “Sometimes you lose and you don’t know why, and sometimes you lose and you don’t know how to explain it.



“We were in control for the most part, our defenders were fantastic and dominated everything, we did a lot of attacking work and created many scoring chances.

“If the match had ended in a draw, we would have left feeling frustrated because we did more, so imagine how we feel after the loss.

“I don’t know why we lost, and I can’t justify it, because the team played very well in all aspects.”

He sarcastically added: “I congratulate Real Betis, they played for the draw and came away with the big prize.”

Sports.title: Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi both BANNED and fined by Uefa for ‘offensive gestures’ aimed at rival fans
Sports.content:
MASON GREENWOOD and Matteo Guendouzi have both been hit by bans and fines from Uefa.

It comes after the Fenerbahce pair were involved in a heated exchange and then brawl on the pitch following the club’s 3-2 aggregate win over Lyon in the Champions League play-offs last month.



The duo both played for Lyon’s rivals Marseille in Ligue 1, but ex-Arsenal star Guendouzi was seen sticking his finger up and shouting “Allez l’OM” (“Go Marseille”) towards Lyon fans.

That saw the midfielder confronted by a man in Lyon colours as a mass brawl, which involved ex-Manchester United star Greenwood, erupted on the pitch.



This was followed by a brawl between both sides in the tunnel.

A Uefa investigation into the incident has now seen fit to slap the pair with punishment.



Guendouzi, 27, was punished for “insulting others present at the match, provoking spectators and for violating the basic rules of decent conduct”.

He has been slapped with a four-game ban in Europe, two of which are suspended “subject to a probationary period of one year”, and a fine of £43,000 (€50,000).

Meanwhile, Greenwood, 24, was given a one-match suspended ban for “violating the basic rules of decent conduct” over the same length of time as his team-mate and fined £26,000 (€30,000).

Speaking after the game, in which he was repeatedly booed by Lyon fans, Guendouzi said he felt “disrespected” by fans who were taunting him with “insults” about his family.

Sports.title: ‘Barcola going to struggle to get a game’: Carragher fears for £123m man as Gakpo shines just days after nearly quitting
Sports.content:
LIVERPOOL legend Jamie Carragher reckons Bradley Barcola is facing a huge battle to break into the starting line-up.

The Frenchman, 24, completed a £123million move from Paris Saint-Germain before the transfer window slammed shut.



And Barcola came off the bench to make his debut as Liverpool notched a 2-0 win over Ipswich Town thanks to a brace from Alexander Isak.

But fellow winger Cody Gakpo caught the eye by claiming two assists in the victory at Portman Road.



The Dutchman’s stunning performance came a matter of days after Liverpool blocked a mega-money switch to Manchester City.

And Carragher reckons the Reds’ last-gasp decision to stave off bids could be bad news for their latest recruit.



In a social media post shared on X, the former defender, 48, said: “Barcola is going to struggle to get a game with this version of Gakpo.”

Liverpool fans quickly backed Carragher’s claim after watching the former PSV Eindhoven cause chaos for Ipswich’s backline.

Gakpo looked like he was on his way through the Liverpool exit door before boss Andoni Iraola and Reds chiefs pulled the plug.

He wanted to head to Man City in a blockbuster deal after snubbing advances from Tottenham.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But Liverpool chose to keep Gakpo, 27, after failing to find a replacement and he now appears to be forming an exciting partnership with Isak.

Having been the provider when the Swede netted against Nottingham Forest last weekend, he also found the striker with two inch-perfect passes at Ipswich.

Liverpool skipper Virgil van Dijk stressed the importance of keeping Gakpo on Merseyside after beating the Tractor Boys.

The centre-back told Sky Sports: “Cody was outstanding. He’s important for us and he will be important this season as well.

“He showed it today, last week as well with the assist and over the last couple of years.”



Gakpo also hinted that he was not furious after being told he would stay at Anfield.

He revealed: “Hopefully we will do many beautiful things together. I am happy.”

Liverpool’s win over Ipswich allowed them to move into the Premier League’s top five ahead of a weekend full of action.

Sports.title: I was in awe of Morgan Rogers aged FOUR & watched him terrorise 13 year olds aged six… £117m Chelsea star is special
Sports.content:
MORGAN ROGERS has been terrorising defenders since he was FOUR.

The man who first spotted the talent of Chelsea’s £117million signing is adamant that the England international stood out from very young.



And on Sunday Rogers heads to Arsenal — who also wanted to sign him this summer — hoping to continue the Blues’ 100 per cent start to this season.

The Gunners were unwilling to go much above the £80m they offered Aston Villa for the attacker and it could come back to haunt them at the Emirates.



Rogers, 24, started his amazing journey in his home town of Halesowen in the West Midlands.

Birmingham cult hero Paul Tait organises soccer schools in the south of the city and remembers the day Rogers first crossed his path.



He said: “I ran — and still run — a Saturday morning coaching course for kids in Halesowen. Morgan’s parents brought him in when he was four.

“From the outset, he was a different level to everyone else. Even at that age. His dribbling. Awareness. Speed. He could kick with both feet. His movement. I was in awe of him.”

Tait, a teen prodigy for Birmingham back in the day, moved Rogers up the groups until he was embarrassing the ten to 13-year-old section at about six.

And Tait, 55, had links with the late, respected talent spotter Steve Hopcroft, who worked at Birmingham before moving to West Brom and then Villa.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Tait said: “I used to really like the Albion set-up back then. I formed a link with them through Steve — who sadly passed away a few months ago — and Mark Harrison, who was then the Baggies’ academy manager.

“Any player I thought would warrant further development, I took them there. Morgan went and after one session Hoppy rang and said, ‘We want him’.”

Rogers was playing for local team Halas Hawks by this stage and had to sacrifice Saturday mornings with Tait.

Tait said: “I just asked the kids to go out there and express themselves. I think that’s how he thrived. He’s gone on record saying he could do anything he wanted and enjoyed it.

“When players join academy set-ups, they mould them into what they want — into robots, a lot of them. I just give them the opportunity to be free and play with a smile on their face, which is what he did.”



Rogers moved from the Baggies to Manchester City’s academy before Middlesbrough signed him in July 2023.

When he was snapped up by Villa in the 2024 winter window for an initial £8m, there were some internal doubts before manager Unai Emery pressed the green light.

Tait revealed: “I spoke to Hopcroft about Morgan nine months or so before Villa signed him.

“They weren’t too enamoured with him at this stage. They thought he’d ‘dropped off a bit’. They’d watched him and were umming and ahing. The next thing you know, they went and bought him.

“It shows what can happen in football. It’s about maybe having that bit of luck — or a manager who has faith in you.”



And then some. Rogers was Emery’s go-to guy within days of him arriving at Villa Park from Teesside.

A trademark of Emery’s sides is the use of a free spirit — someone allowed to pop up anywhere along the frontline.

That took Rogers back to his roots, and led to Villa banking a whopping profit on the player, even with Boro cashing in on a hefty sell-on clause.



Tait added: “To get the best out of him, you have got to let him do what he was doing at Villa.

“He can find space. He’s intelligent. He knows where to go on a pitch. You don’t want to turn him into a regimented player. Xabi Alonso is a top manager and I’m sure he won’t.

“His work ethic is very good. He’s not one-dimensional. He is a big, strong boy, 6ft 3in. He doesn’t get pushed off the ball.

“With Cole Palmer — who has something to prove after not going to the World Cup — they will work well together. But as for Chelsea, I am not sure. I don’t know what to expect of them.

“Gone are those days when you knew what you were getting and who would start. The Terrys, Lampards, Drogbas.



“They now have that many players, you can’t keep track, and loads of youngsters who are loaned out. It’s a massive business, Chelsea.

“So, it does worry me a bit for Morgan and how it’s going to pan out. What is their identity? But I have every confidence in his ability.

“It’s been some journey for him and I truly hope he goes on to smash it at Stamford Bridge. It’s amazing to think back to all those years ago, when he was a little lad running around in mud in Halesowen having fun.



“Then winning the Europa League with Villa, playing for England, starring for Chelsea and costing £117m.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Did I think that he’d go on to do all that? No, of course not. But his talent shone through like a beacon.

“So, no one could have predicted it. But did I think it was possible? One hundred per cent — yes.”

Sports.title: Eagle-eyed fans convinced Man Utd match uncovered as one of Mike Dean’s controversial Premier League ‘mini-games’
Sports.content:
EAGLE-EYED fans are adamant they have found a Premier League clash where referee Mike Dean amused himself by playing mini-games.

The former official, 58, admitted he would go as long as possible without using his whistle and stay in the centre circle during an appearance on Jamie Vardy’s podcast.



Dean’s stunning claims have left Premier League sides irate, with some launching internal probes and trawling through video footage.

And West Brom’s 1-0 win over Manchester United in March 2016 has been pinpointed as a showdown where the ex-ref let his mind wander.



Video journalist Adam Clery has revealed he spent a day scouring through Dean’s performances.

During United’s defeat at the Hawthorns, when Juan Mata was sent off, the man in the middle managed to get through the first 19 minutes of the contest without blowing his whistle.

And West Brom went on to bag their first home win over the Red Devils for 32 years as Salomon Rondon grabbed the only goal of the now-controversial encounter.

Fans are convinced Dean allowed a number of poorly-timed tackles to go unpunished because of setting himself a personal challenge.

One said: “I remember this game and that red card was ridiculous.”

Another added: “United should sue the league.”

A third chimed in: “And there it is.”

A fourth noted: “Disgrace.”

And a fifth claimed: “As someone who regularly bets on fouls, this genuinely is scandalous.”

Dean’s admission stunned crew members working on Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party.

A show insider exclusively told SunSport: “We didn’t think he was being serious.



“It felt like he just wanted to be one of the lads and say some funny stuff. It felt like he wanted to have a bit of banter to be one of the lads.”

Dean broke his silence after the bombshell comments by releasing a statement.

It read: “Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the laws of the game to the best of my ability.

Sports.title: Serena and Venus Williams suffer agonising US Open doubles defeat
Sports.content:
Serena and Venus Williams turn back the clock to defeat Maya Joint and Chan Hao-Ching in a US Open women's doubles first-round epic.

In a fight to the finish, the Williams sisters rallied to force a third set tie-breaker in which they blew a 5-0 lead before falling to Joint and Chan 6-3 6-7 (8-6) 7-6 (10-7) in three hours and two minutes.

The legendary sister act were playing their first Grand Slam together since the 2022 US Open, and 27 years after they first won the title.

The comeback, which Serena said was at the suggestion ​of her daughter, carried the weight of more than two decades: 14 Grand Slam doubles titles together, two US Open crowns, three Olympic gold medals, and another 30 Grand Slam singles titles between ​them.

But it ended up being quite the summer for Joint, the 20-year-old Australian, who defeated Serena on Centre Court at Wimbledon in the women's singles before facing her in front of 23,000 adoring fans at Arthur Ashe Stadium on Friday night.

"Being able to play against such legends of the game is super special," said Joint on court.

"I'm lost for words to think of it," Joint continued. "She's my ​idol, both of them. I grew up in Michigan so I always looked up to ⁠them. Being able to play them twice is amazing."

It was certainly an occasion worthy of wild cards Serena, 44, and 46-year-old Venus were given as their every winner was cheered to the rafters of a packed stadium.

And there could be more to come from the 23-time Grand Slam champion after ESPN commentator Caroline Wozniacki revealed she believes Serena wants to return to singles next year.

They might have a combined age of 90 but the Williams' rolled back the years at times, and all of Ashe was on its feet when a penetrating Venus volley was put away by Serena's swinging winner.

But two breaks of Serena's serve - which had looked in good shape at Wimbledon and in her mixed doubles run-out with Carlos Alcaraz last week - cost them the first set.

They hit back in the second set tie-break, finally converting a fifth set point when a Joint overhead floated long.

The decider also rumbled into a tie-break, the the first time the duo had been past 5-5 in a third set since 2001.

But they stumbled badly in sight of the finishing line and a Chan volley ended the much-anticipated comeback.

The US Tennis Association said the sisters would not be available for comment following their defeat.

Sports.title: Greaves makes more history with win at Czech Darts Open
Sports.content:
Beau Greaves made more darting history as she became the first woman to win a match on the PDC's European Tour - a feat that secured her a second-round clash with Luke Humphries at the Czech Darts Open.

The 22-year-old rallied from 3-1 down to beat Daryl Gurney 6-4 in Prague on Friday night and will now play world No 2 Humphries in the last-32 on Saturday evening, with the winner meeting Nathan Aspinall or Andrew Gilding in round three on Sunday afternoon.

Greaves' latest landmark moment follows becoming the first woman to hit a nine-darter on the PDC Pro Tour, against Mensur Suljovic back in February, and the first to win a PDC ranking title, doing so when she edged Michael Smith 8-7 at Players Championship 11.

She was also the first woman to qualify for a European Tour event when she reached last month's Hungarian Darts Trophy.

Image: Gurney had pipped Greaves in a first-round match at the 2026 World Darts Championship at Alexandra Palace (Pic credit: PDC)

Greaves lost to Rob Cross in the first round in Budapest despite averaging 104 but her run in Prague will now last at least one more match after pinning double one to defeat Gurney, a player she had suffered a narrow 3-2 loss to in round one of the 2026 World Championship.

Greaves 'loving the experience', will 'be ready' for Humphries

Greaves said after a contest in which she won three straight legs in 14, 13 and 11 darts: "It feels amazing. It's just so nice to win a game, I was so nervous at the start, I don't know why. It took me so long to get settled.

"It means loads to me, the crowd's fantastic. It's such a tight stage and you feel so much from the crowd. I'm really enjoying it and loving the experience."

The Yorkshirewoman showed tremendous fight to respond from an early two-leg deficit once Gurney produced a 144 checkout - the same finish which had helped him see off Greaves at Alexandra Palace late last year.

Image: Luke Humphries is Greaves' second-round opponent in Prague

On facing Humphries next, a player she met at the 2025 UK Open, Greaves added: "I've played Luke on the big stage before so I know what to expect, he's world class so I'm going to have to play a lot better than I did tonight.

"What more do you want than on a Euro Tour to play one of the best players in the world? I'll look forward to it and I'll be ready."

Littler to begin campaign on Saturday

Elsewhere on Friday, Niko Springer averaged 102 while routing Martin Homola 6-0 to book a second-round meeting with world No 1 Luke Littler.

Springer said of his showdown with Littler: "I have nothing to lose to be honest. I'm feeling very confident. Of course it will be hard, but it's best of 11, so let's go, I'm ready."

Image: Luke Littler gets his Czech Darts Open campaign under way on Saturday against Niko Springer

Joe Cullen, Dirk van Duijvenbode and Cross were big-name casualties, dumped out by Stephen Burton, Mario Vandenbogaerde and Keane Barry respectively.

Humphries, who, like Littler, received a bye to round two as one of the 16 seeded players, has won the last two Czech Darts Open titles, thrashing Kim Huybrechets 8-1 in the 2024 final and then seeing off Josh Rock 8-5 last year.

'Cool Hand' is targeting a fourth victory in five years at this event having overcome Cross 8-5 in the 2022 final.

Michael van Gerwen and Gerwyn Price are also among the seeds in Prague and will take on Vandenbogaerde and Callan Rydz respectively on Saturday night in the Czech capital.

Sports.title: Hunt runs season's best to take third in Diamond League 200m
Sports.content:
Amy Hunt: British sprinter runs season's best 200m time to take third in Diamond League Athletics meet in Brussels

Great Britain's Amy Hunt ran a season's best in the women's 200m at the final Diamond League event of the year as she took third place in Brussels

Great Britain's Amy Hunt ran a season's best in the women's 200m at the final Diamond League event of the year as she took third place in Brussels.

Hunt's time of 22.16 was outstripped by race winner - and reigning Olympic 100m champion - Julien Alfred of St Lucia (21.79) and America's Kayla White (22.00).

Another Brit, Success Eduan, came seventh of the eight runners after clocking 23.06 in Belgium.

Hunt won four gold medals at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham this summer

Hunt was the poster girl of the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham this summer with her four gold medals and bubbly personality winning her legions of fans.

The 24-year-old topped the podium individually in the 100m and 200m in the Midlands, while she won gold as part of the women's and mixed 4x100m relays.

Elsewhere in Brussels on Friday night, European 400m men's gold medalist Matthew Hudson-Smith, of Great Britain, finished fifth in his event.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Duplantis in injury scare ahead of World Athletics Ultimate Championships

Sweden's pole vault world record-holder Armand Duplantis was forced to pull out of the Diamond League final with back tightness, a week before the inaugural World ‌Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest.

Duplantis said: "The worst possible thing to do is having to pull out of a competition. The fans wanted to see a good show and I wish I could deliver that. Unfortunately, I can't right now.

"My head is everywhere right now. It's super difficult, but that's life, that's the life of an athlete. I try to stay calm and positive. We will see if I can make the Ultimate Championships. I don't have the answer right now."

The World Athletics Ultimate Championships is a new biennial event which sees world champions, Olympic champions, Diamond League winners and other leading athletes compete against each other for shares of a $10m (£7.87m) purse.

Armand Duplantis' army of fans will hope he is fit for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest next weekend

Each individual ​champion will secure $150,000 (£110,865), the biggest winner's ​cheque in track and field history.

Noah Lyles, the men's 100m champion at the 2024 Paris Olympics, will not take part, having ended his season early due to injury - but he still plans to travel to Hungary.

"I am still ​going to be at Ultimate Championship. I still do have ​parties to throw and things to do behind the scenes to help support ​the athletes," Lyles said.

"I still think that this is going to be an ⁠amazing competition, and I'm excited to watch that. And I'm even more excited to see what the future is going to bring."

Sports.title: How influencers at US Open are testing boundaries of tennis etiquette
Sports.content:
A huge discussion around tennis etiquette has been sparked at the US Open due to the disruption caused by a growing number of content creators and influencers at Flushing Meadows.

The number of content creators who have been accredited to cover this year's final Grand Slam of the year has doubled from last year in a move by organisers to reach new audiences. Yet the noise and disturbance caused by them in the stands as been felt by players on court.

Chair umpire Kader Nouni admonished a group of influencers in a suite for recording a video in the middle of a point, while another incident saw a creator using the use of a bright portable ring light to take photos.

Meanwhile, in Naomi Osaka's second-round victory, chair umpire Marijana Veljovic asked fans several times to be quiet.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Naomi Broady and Ryan Harrison try to teach some UK influencers how to play tennis at the US Open

Some players have questioned whether the push for online engagement has gone too far with two-time champion Osaka saying: "I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport.".

"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette."

The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning spectators no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.

And since Osaka's opening match, there has been increased messaging on screens reminding people to refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights.

Some of the behaviour 'disrespectful'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports tennis panel discusses the best fashion so far at the US Open

American and third seed Jessica Pegula has said some of the behaviour has been "disrespectful".

"I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," she said. "But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.

"People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful."

Celebrities have long been ubiquitous in the stands - from A-list stars to US President Donald Trump - as the ultra-wealthy shell out thousands of dollars for seats to get through Flushing Meadows' doors.

But the growing love affair between influencers and the premier ⁠American tennis event has caused some growing pains.

World No 4 Coco Gauff welcomed the influx of new fans but said they should respect the traditions of tennis.

"I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," she said.

"But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans.

"I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport."

Eliza Wastcoat is an influencer who has a passion and knowledge for tennis. She has even launched her own social media channel exploring the intersection of tennis and fashion.

Wastcoat, who moved to America to attend the prestigious Lehigh University, and began her professional career at a creative agency, believes there is room to grow the game but only if organisers and influencers can work together.

"There is a space in tennis for influencers and content creators to be welcomed into the sport and reach new audiences, but I think there's ways in which the sport can do that which includes content creators and influencers who appreciate the sport itself and the etiquette of it and for those who are maybe new and are bringing new audiences in," said Wastcoat, who served as a Wimbledon ball kid when she was younger.

"I do think it's the responsibility of both the brands, the tournaments and the individuals coming to read up a little bit and understand the etiquette of the type of sporting event they're going to.

"Tennis has really opened up its doors to change but ultimately players need some quiet and the ability to concentrate.

"We all want tennis to grow so inviting people in and making it an all-round experience is great for the game, so it's just an opportunity to further educate people about the game on what tennis is."

A learning curve for the USTA

The United States Tennis Association said it wanted fans to have an "incredible time" while ensuring they did not interfere with the action.

"We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited," read a statement from the governing body.

Sports.title: Lawrence leads at halfway stage in Switzerland as he aims to emulate Ballesteros
Sports.content:
Defending champion Thriston Lawrence reeled off six birdies in a row and then made an excellent par save from a bunker to secure the lead at the halfway stage of the Omega European Masters as he looks to emulate the late, great Seve Ballesteros.

Ballesteros is the only player to win this event three times since it became a DP World Tour tournament in 1972, doing so in 1977, 1978 and 1989 - but Lawrence has a chance to do likewise having triumphed at Crans-sur-Siere in 2022 and then again last season.

The South African carded a bogey-free, seven-under 63 on Friday to reach 13 under par and take a two-shot advantage over Germany's Jeremy Paul and Spain's Ignacio Elvira - who shot a round-of-the-day 62 - into the weekend in Switzerland.

Japan's Keita Nakajima sits fourth on 10 under with England's Paul Casey among a group of three players in a share of fifth on nine under with 36 holes remaining.

Casey's compatriot Harry Hall reached 10 under through nine holes of his second round after five front-nine birdies saw him go out in 30, only for a hip injury to then hamper him as he bogeyed three of his final five and slipped to seven under, six shots off the pace.

Image: Lawrence is a five-time winner on the DP World Tour, including twice at the Omega European Masters

Lawrence: I've been playing well all year

Starting at the 10th, Lawrence parred five of his first six holes around a birdie at 13 before he ignited from the 16th when a superb tee shot left him a tap-in birdie.

The 29-year-old picked up shots at his next five holes, too, with highlights including draining from over 40 feet at the first and then holing from off the green at the second.

Lawrence was unable to add to his birdie haul across the last third of his round but saved par at five when he chipped in from the sand - his second attempt to get out of that hazard having initially used the putter to no avail.

Lawrence, without a top-10 finish since March, said afterwards: "I've played well all year. I've just been unfortunate so many times, missing the cut by one shot four or five times. I feel like I've been playing well, but mentally, I'm in a much better space.

"Seeing birdies and putts go in, I feel like you gain confidence from that. Coming back to a place I love is just extra confidence."

Sports.title: Star-studded London City cruise to win over Man Utd
Sports.content:
London City Lionesses started their star-studded era and the new Women's Super League season with a comfortable 2-1 win over Manchester United.

Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas made her debut for the club but despite the Spain international drawing a sell-out crowd at Hayes Lane, it was an own goal from Julia Zigiotti that opened the scoring.

The midfielder wrestled with Alanna Kennedy in the box before inadvertently guiding a header into the back of her own net to score the first goal of the 2026/27 campaign.

London City cruised into control of the fixture from there on, keeping United at arm's length throughout, before a moment of magic from Danielle van de Donk with a neat flick doubled the lead and sealed all three points for the hosts with under 10 minutes to go.

United substitute Simi Awujo tucked away a late consolation goal with virtually the last kick of the game and their only shot on target, highlighting the chasm in standards between the two sides with the talent London City now have at their disposal.

Rosa Kafaji, Mapi Leon, Putellas and Janni Thomsen were the fresh faces included and impressed - while Mary Earps and Kadidiatou Diani were unused on the bench - as an exciting new era got off to the perfect start while owner Michele Kang watched from the stands.

The key moments from Hayes Lane...

9: GOAL! Zigiotti's own goal gives London City the lead

49: SAVE! Kafaji forces a good save from Tullis-Joyce with a long-range shot

64: INJURY! Lucia Corrales goes off injured while clutching shoulder

82: SUPERB! Van den Donk's flick doubles London City's lead to seal three points

90+10: CONSOLATION! Awujo grabs late goal with United's only shot on target

WATCH: All the goals from Hayes Lane!

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danielle van de Donk pulls off a superb flick to give London City Lionesses a 2-0 lead against Manchester United.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Simi Awujo smashes it home to grab a late goal for Manchester United against London City Lionesses.

Maestre: We were very dominant

London City Lionesses boss Eder Maestre:

"Starting with a win is very important to keep building confidence.

"I think we were very dominant through the whole game. I really think we deserved this win. I hope this kind of result makes the difference in the way we can keep playing in the next games we have.

"That's the identity we want - that's why I'm very proud of the team.

"Sometimes you need to take some risks to play in that way. The team played with the togetherness that I think are going to be the most important value to respect.

"I think we are one step closer to hitting the targets. I'm very excited and very happy."

'We were not us,' says Olid

Manchester United boss Eva Olid:

"I think none of us are happy with the first half. We were not us.

"Nothing that we have been working on was happening in the first half.

"In the half-time, it was me saying to them, this is not us, we need to have confidence, belief, show we want the ball, that has to be us.

"There was a change in the second half but at the end but I said at the end that needs to be 90 minutes. It's not enough just 40 minutes trying to have the ball."
