Endo's fitness woes also saw him miss out on the World Cup in heartbreaking fashion, suffering a foot injury on the eve of the tournament, which then led to him announcing his retirement from international football.

His teammate Chiesa, meanwhile, struggled for minutes under Arne Slot and it appears it will be the same story under Iraola.

He made just five starts last season, but previously declared his aim to revive his Liverpool career under new management this season.

Sports.title: 'The most competitive league in the world? Don't be ridiculous. It's rigged': Angry insiders doubt whether Aston Villa, Newcastle, Everton and Co can ever break the Premier League's glass ceiling and challenge the 'arrogant', free-spending 'Big Six'
Sports.content:
'The most competitive league in the world? Don't be ridiculous. It's rigged': Angry insiders doubt whether Aston Villa, Newcastle, Everton and Co can ever break the Premier League's glass ceiling and challenge the 'arrogant', free-spending 'Big Six'

More than anything, it’s the utter sense of resignation that strikes you. There is anger, too.

After a summer that has seen our big Premier League clubs spend and exchange players with all the dignity of the Wolf of Wall Street trading floor, the mood among many of our rank and file top-flight clubs is unanimous.

‘It feels like it’s over for us,’ says one Premier League executive. ‘They say this is the most competitive league in the world. Don’t be ridiculous. It’s not allowed to be. The rules make sure of that.’

The spend in the Premier League this summer was a record £3.49billion. Half of that was spent in deals between top-flight clubs. It’s a story of a league that is now so extraordinarily wealthy that – outside of Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Barcelona – the only clubs rich enough to buy its players are its own.

What that says about the competitiveness of the big European competitions going forward is one thing – English clubs dominated last year – but it’s the increasingly skewed landscape of the Premier League that is now concerning many.

Across English football this week – from executives to coaches to scouts and recruitment specialists – the mood has reflected an environment that has perhaps changed for ever.

Chelsea paid £117million to take the England international Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa

While Arsenal took Newcastle talisman Bruno Guimaraes for £75m

Recruitment from the pyramid of the English game, for example, is now desperately low. Of those players taken from the Championship by Premier League clubs this window, the vast majority were from the three clubs relegated last season.

‘Clubs no longer have the patience to see investments in EFL players pay off over time,’ explains one recruiter at a big club. ‘They want results immediately and they want impact and star names. There is an arrogance from our big clubs and it’s damaging.

‘Signing players is about taking a chance but modern clubs would rather spend £130m on a big name or take someone from clubs lower down in the Premier League who have already done the hard work for them.’

That in itself is an emerging trend. Clubs like Brentford, Bournemouth and Brighton have established recruitment models that are the envy of the so-called 'Big Six'. They sign unknown players for small sums before selling them to top-end rivals for vast numbers. Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton to Spurs is a good recent example.

It’s a practice that on the surface works at both ends. Big clubs get oven-ready players and the smaller clubs make handsome transfer profits. But it’s also a trend that serves to keep the status quo in place on the field. It’s here that the frustration turns to anger.

‘There are well-run clubs doing things the right way who have owners with money yet they are not allowed to spend it,’ adds another Premier League executive. ‘Brentford and Brighton got more points than Chelsea last season. But they are not allowed to spend as much even if they have it.

‘You should never confuse sustainability with competitiveness. We are not competitive. We are not allowed to be by the rules that are essentially endorsed by the big clubs.’

Current spending rules are complicated but broadly speaking allow clubs to spend 85 per cent of what they earn on players, wages and football staff. If you play in Europe, it’s 70 per cent under UEFA’s regulations. It’s this that causes the resentment.

Clubs like Brighton sign unknown players for small sums before selling them to top-end rivals for vast numbers. Jan Paul van Hecke to Spurs is a good recent example

Brentford got more points than Chelsea last season. But they are not allowed to spend as much as them

‘Brighton have got very close,’ says a source who has worked at three top-flight clubs. ‘But they are stuck in a cycle of relative success which is not really success at all in terms of winning things. They are a great club. Well run with a fabulous stadium and training ground.

‘But there is no point anybody buying them because no matter how much money is pumped into it, they wouldn’t be able to spend it on the pitch. Clubs like them and Bournemouth have such limited capacity for growth.’

Another source puts it rather more bluntly. ‘The rules were once worthy and designed to stop people behaving like idiots,’ he says. ‘Sadly the rules have now become a device to stop there ever being a level playing field. The big clubs earn big and spend big. The others don’t and can’t. It’s fundamentally rigged.’

Last November’s vote on new spending rules by top-flight clubs was carried by 14-6, the very minimum required. The dissenters were, not surprisingly, Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds.

At the same time, a proposal to introduce a system of 'anchoring' – where spending by any club could not exceed five times the money earned in the previous season by the league's bottom club from prize money, TV fees and collective commercial income – was supported by only seven clubs and therefore thrown out. The dissenters viewed it as in effect a wage cap.

'The votes are hard,’ reveals someone from inside the room. ‘You have the top six clubs who vote the way it suits them and then the ones who think they may have a chance of becoming one.

‘Everton are a great example of that. The new stadium they think will lead to new revenues and new commercials. And then the new clubs who have been promoted will understandably vote that way too.

‘They just want their £100m for coming up and don’t wanna p*** off Man United as they may need to loan a player from them. It’s a mess and all of this is accelerated and compounded by the media.

‘They say, “They haven’t spent” or “They have had a bad window”. We will spend right up the limit but the truth is that our limits are different and that isn’t fair is it?’

‘Brighton have got very close (to the big teams),’ says a source who has worked at three top-flight clubs. ‘But they are stuck in a cycle of relative success which is not really success at all'

Everton believe they can crash the Big Six thanks to their new stadium, which will lead to new revenues and new commercial opportunities

In an interview with the True Faith Newcastle United Podcast this week, the Magpies’ chief executive David Hopkinson attempted to outline the way forward for a club awash with Saudi Arabian riches that it cannot spend.

Having lost Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali this summer, Newcastle are perhaps the best example of a club that feels it’s being held back on a short lead by the league in which it plays.

Hopkinson talked of growing revenues by 50 per cent between now and 2030. He talked of new commercial revenue streams and sponsorship deals but that figure feels wildly optimistic. ‘We are going to catch up from behind,’ he said bullishly. ‘We have a plan.’

Inevitably that plan must include a new stadium at some stage. This is what has launched Tottenham into the stratosphere when it comes to income and this is what Everton are hanging a blue hat on too. ‘We need more stadium capacity because that capacity is revenue,’ Hopkinson said.

Buried within all this, however, was something else that impacts directly on supporters and not in a good way. It’s another direct trickle down of the League’s restrictions on spending.

Hopkinson talked of ‘VIP hosting opportunities’ and a demand for a ‘higher priced product’. Often what this means is a move to ease out regular fans in a bid to squeeze in those wiling to pay through the nose for what they view as a premium corporate match-day experience.

It is symptomatic of a need to push at the edges of what clubs feel they can get away with in a bid to eke a few more quid from their paying customers.

‘We have had to put regular ticket prices up so that means our fans suffer,’ says a third Premier League chief. ‘We have to do anything we can to try and create a little more revenue that we can then invest in the squad. But it’s still nowhere near what the big clubs can do.

Newcastle's chief executive David Hopkinson is bullish about his club's hopes. ‘We are going to catch up from behind. We have a plan,' he said this week

But the club sold midfielder Sandro Tonali to Tottenham this summer, along with Anthony Gordon to Barcelona and Guimaraes to Arsenal

‘And this pressure to compete can promote clubs gambling with that they have and pushing at the margins. It leads clubs into trouble.’

Maybe the best example of this is Aston Villa, a club whose manager Unai Emery spoke eloquently about the limitations of the rules last season.

‘Financial control rules came to football to avoid bankruptcies and payment defaults with a good purpose,’ said Emery. ‘But this good tool will become a limitation.’

Villa have been successful under Emery. They won the Europa League last season and are about to play Champions League football for a second time in recent years. But their wage bill has rocketed in that time – breaching 90 per cent wages to turnover ratio at one point – while they, along with Chelsea, Nottingham Forest and Newcastle, have all been found to be in breach of UEFA’s spending rules last July.

It’s this that contributes to the kind of boom-bust experience of some of our more ambitious clubs. Successful one season, less so the next. Villa have, for example, lost more than half of their Europa League winning team in the recent window.

Villa – in the process of increasing the capacity of Villa Park from 43,000 to more than 50,000 – voted in favour of the new rules last November and amid all the rancour a question that often goes unanswered is what spending rules in England’s top division actually should look like.

One suggestion from a southern club was for all squads to have the same wage bill ceiling. The 'anchoring' system would have been a step towards that but that idea never got very far.

Meanwhile, another of our insiders adds: ‘I don’t think subsidies are the answer. I agree with the big clubs on that. Why should Tesco give its profits to the corner shop?

'But I do think owners should be allowed to inject money as equity that can then be spent on the football. It’s not debt. Debt comes with interest and must be repaid. It’s damaging. Equity is not the same at all. It should be allowed.’

‘Financial control rules came to football to avoid bankruptcies and payment defaults with a good purpose,’ says Aston Villa boss Unai Emery. ‘But this good tool will become a limitation’

Finally, a third small suggestion from a club in the midlands.

‘We suggested the wages of a home-grown player be added on the balance sheet as a positive,’ a staffer explains. ‘In other words, not included on your expenditure. That wage could then be spent on another player. It would act as a reward for growing your own. It never got past first base.’

When the Premier League announced their amended spending rules last season, they talked of ‘competitive balance’ and ‘promoting opportunities’. Looking across the landscape today, it’s hard to see evidence of it.

With the league having virtually annexed the fifth Champions League spot for the foreseeable future, seasonal revenues of at least £100m from that competition serves to widen the gap further.

Underpinning it all, meanwhile, is a nagging feeling among many with Premier League experience that the bubble has to burst at some point. The current TV deal is worth £6.7bn and runs until 2028 but with the way football fans consume their favourite sport ever changing, there is likely to be a shifting in the sands at some point.

Those numbers cannot be relied upon for ever and already this season the Premier League are experimenting in Singapore with producing and selling their own content direct to viewers.

Speaking on the Athletic FC podcast this week, Tim Bridge of the Deloitte Sports Business Group said: ‘I feel as though the League is banking on the ability to have the next new revenue kick – either a new broadcast contract or new commercial partner.

‘If that happens, then it’s rosy. But there is an awful lot being predicated on that (positive) future change and that feels new for the Premier League. I would suggest an appropriate approach for the 20 clubs would be to work more closely together to think about what the League is going to look like in 2035.’

This weekend, Dan Ndoye's Nottingham Forest will have hopes of beating Tottenham. In the long-term, however, it is hard to see much interference in the general order of things

Villa lost more than half of their Europa League-winning team in the recent window

Given that we are only five years on from the failed attempts by England’s big clubs to join a European Super League, the prospects of such a collegiate approach being taken feels unlikely.

And so the Premier League rolls on. So the gap between the top and the middle grows wider.

This weekend, Nottingham Forest will have hopes of beating Tottenham and Everton may have a real go at Manchester United. In the long-term, however, it is hard to see much interference in the general order of things, not when the richest six clubs earn more than the rest of the other 14 put together.

‘At past Premier League meetings we have scoffed at the way some Championship clubs work,’ one of our Premier League sources adds. ‘They have been reckless, blowing their own brains out.

‘Are we now on the way to doing the same?’

Sports.title: Unused in the Premier League and almost replaced in the transfer market, Viktor Gyokeres' Arsenal career is at a crossroads. But this is why you'd be foolish to write him off
Sports.content:
The career of Arsenal’s Viktor Gyokeres has reached a crossroads. Even he, a man with a piercing gaze and fierce determination, has been unable to hide his unease of late.

An image of a forlorn Gyokeres arriving at Arsenal’s London Colney training base on Thursday was widely circulated online.

Clutching a black washbag, his demeanour spoke of a man lingering on the outside, searching for a way into Mikel Arteta’s first XI plans.

A more telling example of his frustration came in a pre-season friendly away in Girona last month, when he screamed ‘Max!’ at Max Dowman for failing to pass to him.

Gyokeres is in uncharted territory, more generally. The Swede has not played a single minute in either of Arsenal’s two league matches thus far, against Coventry and Aston Villa.

Villa away, for example, seemed tailor-made for the introduction of the 28-year-old in the second period, Kai Havertz having underwhelmed and with the opposition backline flagging.

It's been a disappointing season so far for Viktor Gyokeres, and an image of the forlorn Swede arriving at Arsenal’s London Colney training base on Thursday was widely circulated online

Gyokeres has been left on the bench in Arsenal's first two Premier League games, with Kai Havertz (left) preferred up front

But, no, he stayed put on the bench. It went against the grain for Arteta. Of the 36 league matches last season in which Gyokeres made the Arsenal squad, the striker featured in every single game.

Twenty-six were starts, the other 10 appearances off the bench. It makes his treatment thus far at odds with how Arteta previously used the forward, who struck 21 goals across all competitions last season.

Chelsea at home on Sunday – a fixture that may well have enormous significance in this season's title race – feels a significant moment for the Swede’s Gunners career.

If he were not to feature in any capacity, the experiences of Aaron Ramsdale and Gabriel Martinelli come to mind.

David Raya’s move to Arsenal in 2023 – initially on loan before signing a long-term contract – saw Ramsdale frozen out and eventually sold to Southampton. Ramsdale had been an important player for Arteta, a mainstay of the first XI. And then he wasn't.

Martinelli, meanwhile, only made 11 league starts last season and was sold to Al Hilal for £60million earlier this week.

With Gyokeres, an interesting subplot was Arsenal’s keenness to bring in a striker this summer.

As Daily Mail Sport reported on Wednesday, it is understood assistant manager Gabriel Heinze reached out to Inter Milan’s Lautaro Martinez – a fellow Argentine – early last week over a potential move.

Inter refused to entertain any kind of deal, the attacker still having three years left on his contract.

The Gunners’ pursuit of Julian Alvarez has been well-documented. That, of course, failed to come off.

So, Arsenal were actively trying to bring a striker into the club, aware of the need for one to supplement Havertz and Gyokeres with Gabriel Jesus out the door.

Write off Gyokeres at your peril. It is easy to forget this is a striker who scored 21 goals in all competitions last season

He also has a track record of overcoming adversity, navigating a difficult start to life in England at Brighton (pictured in 2018) by flourishing at Coventry

It’s now crunch time for Gyokeres, though he can at least tap into his experience of overcoming adversity.

After struggling to break through at Brighton aged 19, the Swede went on loan to Coventry, where he would go on to sign a three-year deal and score 41 goals across 110 appearances in the Championship.

That earned him a move to Sporting Lisbon, taking the Portuguese league by storm, striking 97 goals in 102 matches across all competitions.

He will need to summon that same resilience now to reassert himself in an Arsenal frontline shallow in depth. The route back into Arteta’s plans remains firmly within his grasp.

Tellingly, when Arteta was asked on Friday whether his frontline is ‘world class’, he replied: ‘I love my players, that's all I can say. In the bracket, how you want to put them, I don't know.

‘I think at the end of the season we'll put everybody in their place, and let's trust them. Let's make sure that we are right behind them and we'll do everything we can to help the incredible talent that they have.’

Those words offer little in the way of guarantees for Gyokeres. But they do underline the opportunity in front of him.

Chelsea at home on Sunday could provide the clearest opportunity yet to change the narrative, to remind Arteta and the Arsenal supporters why the club pushed so hard to bring him to north London, battling off Manchester United and others for his signature.

Gyokeres has been here before, overlooked and forced to fight for his place. Soon we will discover whether he can do it again.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso are the king of the Premier League and the pretender to the throne. This is the story of how their remarkable shared history led them to the same touchline - as very different managers
Sports.content:
The photograph has been famous for some time. Two 10-year-old boys stand on a grassy slope at a youth football tournament in France, staring into the camera. It is their first tournament abroad with, Antiguoko, a club from their home city of San Sebastian, in the Basque Country. They will go on to win the tournament.

On the left, Mikel Arteta beams into the camera. He looks smart, in a dark anorak. He is holding what looks like a notebook or a map in a plastic holder. He looks neat and together and stylish even then. He looks as if he cannot wait for all the adventures that life is going to bring him.

On the right, Xabi Alonso looks more uncertain. He wears a wistful, thoughtful expression. He is looking at the camera as if it is a curiosity. He is carrying a rolled-up poster in one hand and what looks like a pennant in the other. His anorak is undone and billows around him. They are different characters but a certain intensity is already apparent in both.

And now the boys are men. And the first thing to say about them is that they have grown up good men, a product of their families and their city and their region.

‘I know I am hardly neutral expressing my opinion on him as a friend and former team-mate,’ Jamie Carragher says of Alonso, ‘but anyone who spends time with Xabi will appreciate that the manner in which he carries himself and presents his vision of the game oozes class.’

Arteta can divide opinion more than his old friend but his instincts are sound and he tries to be fair and just, not only with his players but with everyone he meets.

He is liked by staff and players at Arsenal and if it sometimes feels that he lacks levity, that is because levity is not something he aspires to.

Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso, aged 10, during their time at Antiguoko, a club in San Sebastian. The pair will face off on the touchline at the Emirates this Sunday

The coincidence of Alonso and Arteta growing up together, playing football on Playa de La Concha in San Sebastian, playing for the same youth team, growing into players who faced each other for Liverpool and Everton and now will face each other as managers of Chelsea and Arsenal at the Emirates on Sunday, is endlessly striking.

Both men have led their clubs to successive wins in the early stages of the new season and early predictions are that they and their respective teams are the most likely sides, along with Manchester City, to contest the title this year.

Sunday’s Emirates clash will be their first meeting as managers but it seems likely to be the start of a fierce rivalry.

To add to the fascination of their shared background, Andoni Iraola, the new Liverpool manager, played for Antiguoko at the same time but Alonso and Arteta have risen faster and more prominently. And if their backgrounds unite them, the different paths their careers took exposed them to contrasting influences that have shaped the football their teams play.

Both men have been outstandingly successful already. Arteta took over as Arsenal boss at the end of 2019 when the club was at a low ebb. He brought the club together, dragged it out of the despond that followed the Arsene Wenger years and had the hunger and the drive to survive three consecutive runner-up finishes to beat Manchester City to a first title in 22 years last season.

Those three successive second-place finishes would have destroyed other managers but not Arteta. He did not lose belief in himself or his players. He stuck to his playing principles, he resisted revolution, he kept evolving the side. He played under David Moyes at Everton and cites Moyes’ influence as a lesson in to how to build a club.

Alonso made a spectacular start to his own coaching career, taking over at Bayer Leverkusen in October 2022 and doing the unthinkable by leading them to the first Bundesliga title in their history in 2023-24 without losing a game. Leverkusen’s win halted a run of 11 straight Bayern Munich title triumphs.

Mikel Arteta has turned Arsenal into the dominant force in English football, never losing belief in himself or his players despite three straight second-place finishes

Alonso, meanwhile, will try and replicate his enormous success at Bayer Leverkusen with Chelsea

When the two boys left Antiguoko within a few months of each other in their teenage years, Arteta went to Barcelona and gradually came under the orbit of Pep Guardiola.

Most significantly of all, he became a disciple of Johan Cruyff, the great Dutch player who became one of the most imitated and followed coaches of all time and introduced a kind of ‘total football’ to Barcelona.

‘They changed the world for me,’ Arteta says of his time at Barcelona. ‘It’s like the sky had opened and this was a different sport.

'Johan was the influence of everything when I was at the La Masia academy, all the coaches who were at the academy it was the same. He was the one that injected that vision and that passion and understanding for the game.

‘From there, the game has evolved. Pep took the game and his vision to a different level. Johan is the greatest football person. I fell in love with that Barcelona team of his, I was six or seven, and I fell in love with that team, that way of playing. I had posters, kits, and if Barcelona were losing 1-0, I was going mad and my dad would send me to bed.

‘I learned a lot about the culture of a club when I was there and now, at Arsenal, it’s about the culture I create.

'It’s like drizzle. It’s always raining. You have to have a jacket because if you decide you are going to go without a jacket, you are soaking wet. If you don’t do it every day, the structure cracks.

‘I have high demands but I am realistic, too. What do I expect from one of my kids? That he goes to his room and everything is tidy and he always flushes the toilet and his toothpaste is always in the right place and they eat and they are always dressed? It’s not like this. We want everything perfect but this game is very imperfect.

‘I like to be challenged but if you work with me at Arsenal in the environment we have created at the club, I need you to love what you do because that is why we are here and we have to be contagious.’

Arteta's vision of football was shaped by Barcelona. He idolised Johan Cruyff, and worked for years with Pep Guardiola

Alonso, however, was shaped by a more diverse group of managers, including Rafa Benitez at Liverpool

Alonso’s influences are more diverse. Arteta idolised Cruyff, admired Moyes and worked with Guardiola at Manchester City but Alonso has played for both Guardiola and Jose Mourinho, both Rafa Benitez and Carlo Ancelotti. He has already managed in Germany and Spain, where his reign at Real Madrid was short-lived. Some credit him with being more flexible and pragmatic than Arteta.

‘The data and the information is not everything,’ Alonso says. ‘You have to have knowledge and intuition. You have to have man management. I have had great managers and from each one, I have learned. I have lived with them through good and bad moments and understood why they have made their decisions.

‘It’s not copy, paste. It’s about being authentic, being your own self. Building my own ambition as a coach, taking the best from each one. That is the way you are going to be able to trust me. I want to be open-minded to everything, not just one idea, have different ideas, sticking with your principles.

‘In different countries, you live different things. The more you know, the better you can get. The German way – for the last 20 years, something has been happening in German football. I think it started in 2006 with the World Cup in Germany and the influence of Jurgen Klinsmann.

‘What the German Federation started doing with grassroots and new managers and young managers. The profile of the manager is very brave and intense, physical but with a tactical approach. Julian Nagelsmann, Thomas Tuchel and Jurgen Klopp but there are others, too. I thought it was great what they were doing.’

So if Arteta largely sticks with a 4-3-3 system that has consistently served him well, Alonso mixes styles according to the challenge in front of him.

The basic formation he favours is 3-4-2-1 but against Brighton last weekend, Chelsea won the game 4-3 while recording only 26 per cent of possession. When new goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez was on the ball, 97 per cent of his passes were hit long. As he settles in at Stamford Bridge, that process will be refined.

Sunderland’s Granit Xhaka has played for both managers. He is more complimentary about Alonso than Arteta, which is hardly a surprise given he was the star man for Bayer Leverkusen in their title-winning season and endured some difficult times at Arsenal before and after Arteta’s arrival.

‘Mikel has his philosophy and that’s it,’ Xhaka says. ‘You know this: always change the sides, find the free man, let him jump, for example. Play always with a back four and never change to a back five for example, or never change like a 4-4-2 with two proper strikers. So you had this 4-3-3, with one six and two eights.

‘Xabi is a little bit different. I think that Xabi can play a back four, but he can play as well a back five. What he wants is always two No6s, not running everywhere, or more of the time be in the position. But if you are a coach you need your own philosophy, your own tactics, your own ideas.’

‘Mikel has his philosophy and that’s it,’ Granit Xhaka says of Arteta, under whom he endured some difficult times at Arsenal

‘Xabi is a little bit different,' adds Xhaka of Alonso, who is perceived as a more flexible coach than his boyhood friend

It is the most eagerly anticipated game of the season so far. Chelsea under Alonso look like the great entertainers, despite that possession statistic against Brighton. They will score plenty and concede a few, too.

Alonso appears to have allowed Cole Palmer to rediscover his best form and line him up in a formidable front three with Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro. They will present a test for Arsenal’s redoubtable defence.

Arsenal already look like the team to beat again this season. Their squad is even deeper and even more impressive than it was last season. They have improved from a position of strength. They look, at last, like a team that believes in itself after getting over the line and winning the title.

This is Arteta’s league now. He is the manager of the champions, he is the longest-serving manager in the top flight by a distance, he is the man.

But if there is a pretender, if there is a manager who has the qualities to threaten his dominance, it is the man who was once the boy standing next to him in the photograph all those years ago.

Sports.title: 'I didn't watch Villa when I was injured... it was too difficult': BOUBACAR KAMARA opens up on his 'tough' comeback from injury, what life is like under Unai Emery and why he's optimistic Aston Villa's best days are ahead of them
Sports.content:
Boubacar Kamara puffs out his cheeks and grimaces ever so slightly. The Aston Villa man is one of the best midfielders in the business but still the crash-bang-wallop of the modern Premier League takes his breath away.

Villa’s much-changed team are still looking for their first point and goal of the season after defeats by Brighton and Arsenal, and they travel to Hull on Saturday with the promoted team seeking a third successive win.

Unai Emery has lost six key players and brought in 11 new ones but at least he still has Kamara, probably Villa’s most important player and firmly on the road to full recovery after the second serious knee injury of his career.

But what a challenge it is. According to data from analytics company Skill Corner, in partnership with the SCOUTED platform, the Premier League outstrips every other league in five key physical metrics – distance covered, speed at which a player changes direction, top speeds, explosiveness and intensity.

According to Frank Lampard, one of the greatest midfielders of the Premier League era, the increasing emphasis on athleticism is probably irreversible.

When we put it to Kamara that the modern Premier League is becoming ever more like the NFL, he nods emphatically. ‘Yeah – that’s right,’ he says. ‘Is it as physically demanding as it has ever been in my career? Of course – by far.

The rough and tumble of the Premier League still takes Boubacar Kamara's breath away. ‘Every contact, everyone fights for the ball,' he says

The Frenchman has cemented his reputation as one of the finest midfielders in the Premier League since joining Villa in 2022

‘Every contact, everyone fights for the ball. The striker fights, the goalkeeper fights, everyone wants to win the ball, everyone has become stronger. In some moments during the game, it’s only fighting.’

It is a fight Villa need to win. At Brighton, they were felled early in the bout and never climbed off the canvas, losing 4-0 in a feeble performance.

And though Emery’s men threw a few more punches against Arsenal, it was still the champions who landed the knockout blow to secure a 1-0 victory at Villa Park. Emery’s men have not registered a shot on target this season.

The battles are becoming harder every year. In three full seasons under Emery, Villa have finished fourth, sixth and fourth, qualifying for the Champions League twice, as well as lifting the Europa League.

Even though their work in the transfer market leaves much to be desired, they have also been severely restricted by UEFA rules that seem tailor-made to favour Europe’s wealthiest.

‘It’s really difficult – every year the Premier League is so tough,’ Kamara reflected. ‘You have 10 teams fighting every year to get in Europe.

‘But to keep this mentality and consistency, and to finish every year in the top four or top six, and also to play in Europe every three days, going far in those competitions… it’s really not easy.

‘We saw last year and two years ago that at certain times of the season we were without certain players at crucial times. So when we saw the table at the end of the year we were proud, and we believe we can do even better this season.’

Emery’s long training sessions and even longer stints in the analysis suite have already raised eyebrows among those new players used to lighter regimes at previous clubs.

Life under Unai Emery is intense, and not for everyone. But so many of Villa's players have reached new heights under the Spaniard

Kamara suffered a serious knee injury in an FA Cup tie with Tottenham back in January

The Villa boss leads every day’s training and twice a week, in the afternoons, he will conduct 90-minute briefings. Sometimes, those are followed by individual chats with players.

It is intense stuff and there are unlikely to be many of the new faces in the starting XI at Hull. Yet as Kamara warns, the new players need to get up to speed – and fast.

‘With the meetings, you don’t have a choice – you need to sit and watch,’ Kamara says. ‘In training, every day you have the same task.

‘When new players arrive, they do extra work with Unai’s assistants. They teach them what they need to do so their adaptation can be as quick as possible. We have so many good, intelligent players in the team, too.

‘We will see what the manager wants. In some games, he wants us to play low block with good transitions. In others, he wants us to press high, keep the block high and play a lot of passes. Every game, we change our structure.

‘When we’ve shared the dressing room for three or four years with the same players, we are sad for a day or two but after that we are happy for them.’

As difficult as this start has been for Villa, simply having Kamara around is a bonus.

When he is in the team, Villa’s results are significantly better than when he is not. In that context, it was a huge achievement both to win the Europa League and finish in the top four last season, given Kamara did not play a game after injuring his knee at Tottenham on January.

Not only did he miss Villa’s march to Europa League glory, culminating in the win over Freiburg in Istanbul in May’s final, he also lost the chance of representing France at the World Cup. It was the same story before the 2022 tournament. Kamara is 26 and has yet to represent his country at a major tournament.

'It was difficult the first one or two months after my surgery,’ admits Kamara. ‘You can’t work, you have to stay at home'

‘Mentally it was difficult the first one or two months after my surgery,’ he admits. ‘You can’t work, you have to stay at home, ice treatment, do some exercises.

‘This is why I didn’t watch Villa play during that time, either at the ground or on TV. You want to play then you look at your knee and realise you can’t.

‘You keep going, work, and try not to think about football, think more about family, my kids, my friends. But it’s tough.

‘Before the game in Istanbul, I walked on to the pitch and I wanted to play, but I knew I couldn’t. Afterwards, I sat in my spot in the dressing room and I was a little bit sad, because I couldn’t do anything.

'So yes, in some moments it’s difficult but I tried to keep focused and now it is time to look forward again.’

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: This is the untold behind-the-scenes story of the rumbling Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight talks - and how much the pair stood to lose under disgraceful idea to stage bout in New York
Sports.content:
I remember the first time I reported that cogs were turning on a fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. It was a good while ago – almost 12 years, actually.

The date was December 2, 2014. I’d spoken that evening to Joshua’s promoter, Eddie Hearn, when both his guy and Fury were unbeaten and neither had fought for a world title.

Hearn, then and now, was bullish in spelling out his plan. ‘It is a fight I would love to make next summer,’ he told me. ‘People ask if AJ is ready to fight Fury but, to be honest, is Fury ready to fight AJ?’

It was a nice line for the back page and ultimately good for one thing alone – proving the timeless point that, in boxing, you should only believe it when you see it.

But here we are, trapped in a different version of the same dance all these years on.

Because as of Friday, the fight was on and, according to Hearn, talks had been resurrected to take it to Wembley Stadium. A day earlier it was heading to New York’s Madison Square Garden on November 20 and Joshua’s team were floating the possibility of canning the whole thing in protest.

They were furious that a contract signed three months ago, stipulating a UK venue, was being broken so that Netflix could have a cosier fit with American viewing hours. The Saudi powerbrokers for the fight, led by Turki Alalshikh, were evidently happy to side with the broadcaster, to hell with the British audience for a British fight, and ostensibly that is what sent Hearn and Joshua into a spin.

Twelve years on from when I reported that Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury were in talks to fight each other, the pair are still yet to touch gloves

Fury and Joshua are closer than ever to trading blows, with signatures on contracts, but they are still squabbling on the details

Time will tell if they get their way – Wembley conversations may have reopened, but it isn’t the only factor at play in this game of brinksmanship. Far from it.

I’ve had conversations this week with people around the deal and can flesh out a few of the details behind the chaos, which boils down to a boring three-letter word. Tax.

It’s something Hearn himself has alluded to in interviews this week – he mentioned that tax conditions in the US were unfavourable for Joshua. The information I’ve since received illustrates what that would look like in real language.

In short, it is my understanding that Joshua’s team have somewhere close to 10 million reasons not to want the fight in New York. Explained in a slightly longer form: if it is staged in London, the tax for a pair of non-UK residents would be around 20 per cent and in the US ‘withholding tax’ is around 30 per cent.

That is a significant jump with the purses involved – I’m told Joshua and Fury are in line to receive approximately $100m each (around £74m), so a $10m shortfall on the net amounts they would take back to Dubai and the Isle of Man respectively has not gone unnoticed.

As far as we can tell, Fury has not kicked up a fuss on the US tax. Publicly, anyway. But Joshua’s team viewed it as a hefty pay cut on what he signed, which fed into their wider anger that the fight was being shifted abroad.

Irrespective of which motivation weighed more, it seems that some level of sense might yet prevail – if the fight lands in the UK, that can only be a good thing. Hearn was very much in the right to paint it as a disgrace if it goes anywhere else.

But, again, we are in the realms of believing it when we see it. And especially in consideration of the individuals who hold true power behind this fight. That would be Netflix, who presumably still see greater value in the US, and the Saudi organisers, Sela, who have been steered on this fight by Alalshikh.

If fight is staged in the US, Joshua and Fury are set to pay millions more in tax. Fury and his promoter Frank Warren have not kicked up a fuss on issue - publicly at least

Turki Alalshikh (centre) claimed that he was trying to stage the fight in London back in July, though this may only have been lip service

Alalshikh, you might note, has already performed a curious role in the London saga. It was early July when he began applying pressure to City Hall, flagging that curfews in the capital would need tweaking to enable a US-friendly start time.

Writing on X, his favoured means of communication, he posted: ‘Hopefully a positive statement from the Mayor of London’s office about a later start time if Fury v Joshua is in London, as so far we have been told it is not possible.’

I might add here that the latter sentiment landed as something of a surprise to those on the receiving end – I’m told no request was made by Sela to mayor Sadiq Khan until mid-August. When those conversations did finally occur, sources tell me it was made clear by the mayor’s office that a late start wouldn’t be a hurdle. Khan has since gone public in saying he wants the fight in London.

A plausible theory, held by a few parties, is that the Sela overture was a gesture. A means of being able to claim: ‘We tried.' Lip-service, in other words, and flapping lips in boxing tend to serve no one.

Hopefully this fight proves the exception to the rule. Hopefully it does go to London. Hopefully the pressure applied by Hearn and Joshua, for whatever reason they prioritised, is decisive. Anything else would be an utter sham and a betrayal of British sport.

But this is boxing. And for more than a decade, one excuse after another has been found to keep these two fighters apart – the threshold for tedium was breached long before any contract. If that extends indefinitely, the question of New York or London might be rendered slightly irrelevant.

Sports.title: French tennis star Gael Monfils reveals he's going to work in an OFFICE after playing his last US Open at 40
Sports.content:
French tennis icon Gael Monfils revealed that he will be eschewing traditional post-playing careers such as punditry and working within tennis to take up a job in finance.

The 40-year-old called time on his Grand Slam career when he was despatched in straight sets by rising American talent Learner Tien in their second-round clash on Thursday night.

Monfils was previously treated to a lengthy send-off at his home major Roland-Garros in May, retiring as one of the biggest names in the last 20 years of French tennis.

But rather than parlay his success on the court into a media role, Monfils - who is married to women's tennis star Elina Svitolina - will start a new career in an unexpected field.

'I have a new chapter coming next year,' Monfils told the press after his match. 'I will work in finance. You know, I already signed to work in wealth management in a Swiss company.

'So my next chapter working in office and working in finance. I will always have a look on tennis, because I love the sport. My wife's playing.

Gael Monfils has shared that after retiring, his new career is a world away from the tennis court

'I don't think this next year I will do so much about tennis. But I'll be around definitely no matter what for Elina a little bit, but I will be more a finance guy.'

Monfils, who was ranked as high as world No6 at his very peak and reached two Grand Slam semi-finals in 2008 and 2016, was asked how the new role might translate his tennis skills. The Frenchman's glittering career has been distinguished by his ability to entertain with both his electric shot-making, and ebullient character - but Monfils admitted there was another side to him too.

'Somehow, and I think you should ask my wife, you'd be very surprised, is of course in tennis I am the way I am, but I think she can tell you that she wishes I am like this at home,' he added. 'I think at home I'm a little bit more strict, more serious, completely different.

'(Tennis) is my joy place where I can let my emotion go. Then I'm pretty - it's tough to say, but - I'm really not flexible in a way, that I really like everything done straightaway and a little bit maniac, so it fits that for sure, for my next chapter.

'Tennis is completely different.'

After his match against Tien finished, Monfils was treated to a small ceremony commemorating his career. Smaller than he had experienced in Paris, but special all the same.

'It was just really tough for me,' Monfils said of his decision to retire. 'A couple weeks ago in Paris, couple months ago now, it was really tough, because you don't really know what to expect and how you will really react.

'It was a little bit tougher for me to handle my emotion and play and perform, because I said that I want to say goodbye but be able to perform well.

'In Paris was a little bit tougher, but I felt like I learned a lot. And then it was much better, much easier for me to handle (saying goodbye) here, because here, it was a big one, very important one, and I was super happy that I could actually be here.'

Sports.title: Aryna Sabalenka stops play at US Open to complain about the smell of WEED after claiming a fan was 'smoking' during her third-round match: 'It was so strong'
Sports.content:
Aryna Sabalenka was forced to stop her third-round match against Kamila Rakhimova to complain about someone apparently smoking weed inside the US Open's Louis Armstrong Stadium.

The court is the second-largest of the tournament's showcourts, but despite the venerable setting, Sabalenka was so disturbed by the smell of what she believed to be marijuana that while serving in the third game, she called for umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore's attention after first speaking to her team.

'Someone is smoking weed,' she said as she paused play at 30-0 up to speak Asderaki-Moore. 'Would you mind to (tell them to deal with it) because it's so strong.'

The world No1, who went on to win in straight sets, had been serving at the south end of the stadium, close to where her team were seated in the players' box.

The chair umpire quickly radioed for assistance, making a mysterious snipping signal at her colleagues. Members of US Open staff then headed into the crowd in a bid to find the source of the smell.

The smell of cannabis is not unexpected around the grounds of the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, due to its position inside Flushing Meadows Corona Park, where weed can be smoked legally by those relaxing in the sunshine.

Aryna Sabalenka alleged that a spectator was smoking weed during her US Open match

It is however forbidden, along with all forms of smoking, inside the tournament. The US Open has been contacted for comment.

During qualifying and ahead of the start of the tournament, a number of British players noted the unique smell of the grounds, with Katie Boulter particularly disapproving of how the stink hung around Court 17 - referred to in the Danish media as 'hash court' for how strongly the smell lingers in the air.

‘I have experienced it,’ Boulter, who was knocked out on Wednesday by Karolina Muchova, shared. ‘You got down to the practice courts and down in the park courts, you do smell it a lot.

‘I’m not a huge fan of it. I know a lot of players have complained on specific courts. I’ve played on (Court 17) before and I did smell it during my match. It’s something that I wouldn’t like to smell in the middle of my match.’

In response, the USTA shared the following statement: 'While we can’t control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this facility as a smoke-free environment.

'This includes enforcement by our security and guest services teams when they are made aware of any individual that may be smoking, making them aware that although it may be legal in New York, that smoking is not permitted on parks property, including the tennis center.

'We constantly work with the NYPD and Parks Department, and we believe this has helped to decrease smoking near our fenceline.'

Sabalenka brushed aside world No 92 Rakhimova to continue her straight-sets march

Sabalenka brushed aside world No 92 Rakhimova to continue her straight-sets march towards what she hopes is a third-consecutive US Open title.

And of the earlier incident, she later said with a smile: ‘I was like guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax however you want, but please try not to do it during a tennis match. It’s a bit tricky to handle the smell while you’re trying to compete at your best.

‘But come on guys, I think there is nothing more to say about weed. I’m just asking people not to smoke it next to the tennis court,’ she continued, only to add of her game: ‘Maybe it’s too fast for them, and they want to slow down!’

Despite the early distraction, Sabalenka was able to reset with the minimum fuss and continue to scythe through the opening set.

The second was another matter. Almost double the length of the opener, Rakhimova had grown into the match and tested Sabalenka from the off as she pushed her to deuce four times in her first service game.

Only a strong serving performance, with 10 aces struck across the match, kept her opponent from hunting down a crucial break.

Although joking with the press pack about how ‘high’ being in New York made her feel on Friday, Sabalenka has been a trickier subject after her matches in New York. Wound tight after a challenging summer that has seen her normally ultra-consistence form take a nosedive, her attitude has read as defensive.

In the second set, this mode switched to visible frustration. The world No1 shouldn’t have looked as frustrated as she did as Rakhimova continued to deny her opportunities to break her serve - the win was almost inevitable.

There is a growing sense however, that Sabalenka wants not just to keep going in the tournament, but to wrench back the feeling of dread her opponents would normally sense when seeing her in their section of the draw. Amid a summer of toothlessness as her level has dropped, that was not assured coming into New York.

Slowly but surely, however, she is clawing this back.

Sports.title: Sarcastic Jose Mourinho hits out after Real Madrid's controversial defeat: Kylian Mbappe has 94TH-MINUTE penalty saved - which should have been retaken - as ex-Spurs star scores the winner for Real Betis
Sports.content:
Sarcastic Jose Mourinho hits out after Real Madrid's controversial defeat: Kylian Mbappe has 94TH-MINUTE penalty saved - which should have been retaken - as ex-Spurs star scores the winner for Real Betis

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jose Mourinho suffered the first setback of his second spell as Real Madrid manager as his side were beaten 1-0 by Real Betis, with Kylian Mbappe missing a last-minute penalty.

Real Madrid had won three consecutive league matches to begin the season, following Mourinho's high-profile return to the club.

The first defeat came at the hands of one of Mourinho's former players in Troy Parrott, who he gave his Premier League debut to in 2019 when in charge of Tottenham.

Parrott, who joined Real Betis in a £17million summer move, was on hand to score on the rebound in the 80th minute after Nelson Deossa's header from a corner had been saved by Thibaut Courtois.

Mourinho, who was booked in the 54th minute, thought his side had levelled in the closing stages.

A superb acrobatic volley from Espi from a Vinicius Jnr cross was ruled out after VAR adjudged the forward was offside.

Jose Mourinho suffered the first defeat of his second spell at Real Madrid on Friday night

Kylian Mbappe missed a stoppage time penalty as Real Madrid were beaten 1-0 by Real Betis

Troy Parrott, who was given his Premier League debut by Mourinho, scored an 80th minute winner

Real Madrid, however, were then given the chance to preserve their unbeaten start to the campaign when they were awarded a stoppage-time penalty after a foul on Vinicius.

Mbappe was denied from the spot by a diving save from Alvaro Valles, with the goalkeeper then squaring up and pushing the Real Madrid star as he celebrated the stop.

Footage showed the penalty should have been retaken after a Real Betis player had encroached into the box as Mbappe was striking the ball.

Mourinho insisted post match that his side had deserved to win, while he sarcastically congratulated Betis players and suggested they had been 'smarter' in committing fouls after five Real Madrid players were booked.

'Congrats to Betis, they won the lottery tonight.'

The game was all Real Madrid, we created so many chances, if we drew tonight, we would have been disappointed.

'I might change my mind tomorrow, but today, judging by the feeling on the bench, I don't know why we lost because collectively we played very well.

Mourinho sarcastically congratulated Real Betis players following the match

'I have nothing to reproach any player for regarding their attitude. We deserved to win, but deserving doesn't get you points.

He added: 'Betis players are smarter than Real Madrid players, who are more straightforward.

'In the first play of the game, there was a clear yellow card for a player who fouled Valverde, but Fede stays on his feet, he doesn't even fall.

'Meanwhile Betis players exaggerated every foul so much, that you'd think they need an ambulance from their reactions.'

On his own yellow card, Mourinho added: 'I don't know why I saw a yellow card.

'I accept it.

'I stood up because a Betis player looked like he'd died in front of the bench. I saw a lot of people frustrated with the plays, but I didn't see it myself and I can't comment.'

The slip-up gives rivals Barcelona the chance to establish an early three-point lead on Real Madrid, with the Catalans looking to clinch a third successive LaLiga title.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
