Though the normative coal requirement at power plants is calculated at 3.1 MT every day at 85% plant load factor, officials said the actual requirement is around 2.4 MT.





The monsoon sees supply disruptions every year. The situation starts improving from Sept onwards as rains begin to recede.

While the power ministry did not respond to requests for a reaction, sources said some coal-fired plants had been asked to defer scheduled maintenance to ensure continuity of electricity generation.

World.title: Tetris distances itself from controversial White House 'arcade' games
World.content:
Tetris said on Friday (September 3, 2026) that it did not give permission for the White House to use the game's iconic imagery for a controversial online arcade that the U.S. President Donald Trump administration released on Thursday (September 4, 2026).

"The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of 'Build the Wall' and did not authorize or license the Tetris brand or intellectual property for the game," Tetris told AFP in a statement.

"We are currently reviewing the matter," the statement continued.

A block-stacking game called Build the Wall included instructions to "protect the border from the coming horde".

The arcade-style games and promotional content used by the Trump administration contain images that resemble games created by Tetris and other major game developers including Sega, Microsoft-owned Xbox and the Flappy Bird Foundation.

"At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them," Tetris said in a social media post.

"P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously," the post continued.

Promotional content posted by the White House on social media also included images that resemble trademarks and designs from Microsoft-owned Xbox.

P.S. The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of 'Build the Wall'.



P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously. pic.twitter.com/Fu02khRpT3 — Tetris (@Tetris_Official) September 4, 2026

Microsoft did not respond to requests for comment, and the Sega Corporation couldn't immediately be reached.

The White House released several games Thursday, with a placeholder that teased another one "coming soon."

The web-only games, which were published on the official White House website under a new page called "arcade," sparked condemnation for racist themes and prompted questions about potential copyright violations.

In one clip, the letters from the Sega logo transform into MAGA, a term that stands for Make America Great Again, which President Trump turned into his campaign slogan during his first presidential run for the 2016 election.

A game called "Flappy Bill" features a bald eagle carrying a document in its claws that tries to avoid smashing into columns of various heights, against a background that resembles Washington DC.

"This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the President's many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American," the White House said Thursday in a statement to AFP.

Rights groups criticised the White House.

"Makes me sick. They've been playing games with people's lives for years, now they've made a video game of what they're doing," Amerika Garcia Grewal, co-director of the Frontera Federation in Eagle Pass, Texas, told AFP.

"There's no attention paid to the quality of life for human beings, both those in their game or those in real life. We who live in the borderlands are U.S. citizens and yet are treated with suspicion and violence," she added.

The game designers "have lost touch with what it means to be human and care for others."

Mr. Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken several actions since returning to power aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings.

His White House meanwhile has long used social media stunts to ram home its points and troll liberal opponents, and has sparked a backlash from several artists by using their music without permission.

The White House is trying to convince voters that Mr. Trump's second presidential term has been successful ahead of the midterm election in November. The balance of power in Congress will also be at stake when Americans go to the polls in just over two months.

World.title: From asteroid hunter to Maths wizard, 82 educators to receive National Teachers’ Awards
World.content:
An asteroid hunter. A Maths wizard. A trailblazer in a coal mining community. A Special Olympics hockey coach. These are among the 82 educators from across the country who will receive the National Teachers’ Awards on September 5, 2026. The President of India Droupadi Murmu will confer the awards.

Among the awardees are 48 school teachers, 21 faculty members in higher education, and 13 trainers from the Union Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. Among the faculty in higher education are proponents of Indian Knowledge Systems, including Vaastu Shastra, the Bhagavad Gita, and the integration of Sanskrit with AI.

One of the awardees, Haryana-based Anil Kaushik, known as the ‘Math Wizard’, built a state-of-the-art physical Maths lab containing over 40 original learning models, alongside a 12-section virtual mathematics lab with 30 ‘Harbans puzzles’. He has co-authored textbooks on Vedic Mathematics and published 22 teaching modules on the national DIKSHA portal.

Divyendu Sen from Rajasthan, another recipient of the award, is a teacher in a government school who bridged rural classrooms with deep-space science by training local students to track and hunt asteroids. He has pioneered low-cost solutions, including an AI-enabled Biology education model, a Virtual Biology Laboratory, and ‘Tree Talk’, a QR-based botanical learning system.

Rajasthan-based teacher Vartika Gulati is an awardee who teaches at the Government Girls Upper Primary School in Jaipur. She turns abstract concepts into everyday experiences — teaching Algebra with groundnuts and geometry with kites. Her initiative, ‘Prashno Se Vigyan’ (Science through questions), replaces rote learning with student-led inquiry.

Odisha-based teacher Padaraj Nayak, based at the Government High School, Alipingal, is receiving the award for guiding students to build over 50 prototypes, including a low-cost automatic plate-washing machine that earned a Government of India patent.

Another awardee, Jharkhand-based Munmun Bhattacherjee, working at the Government Middle School in Barmasia, Dhanbad, Bihar, has spearheaded an institutional turnaround in a vulnerable coal mining community. Aligning with the NEP 2020 and NIPUN Bharat goals, she introduced low-cost Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) tools; integrated Children with Special Needs (CwSN); prevented dropouts through home visits; and guided students toward State arts awards, NEET prep, and vocational independence.

Similarly, Maharashtra-based Kavita Gitte, head teacher at the Sane Guruji Nivasi Vidyalaya in Beed, is being felicitated for spending nearly three decades integrating children of migrant sugarcane workers into mainstream schooling via initiatives like ‘Balrakshak’ and ‘Shikshan Aaplya Dari’. As a national softball and baseball coach, she has also guided nearly 210 students to State and national achievements.

Another awardee, Gujarat-based Nitinkumar, converted a resource-constrained tribal primary school in Vansda, Navsari, into a national hub for digital learning. He built a 45-computer IT lab, a 7D VR/AR lab, an offline ‘Rangpur Server’, and a student journalism studio called ‘R NEWS’. His ‘QR Code Book’ project and ‘Touchable PDFs’ reached over 112,000 students across Gujarat during the pandemic.

Goa-based Mahadev Shinde, who is among the national awardees, is a pioneer in adaptive sports at the Gujarati Samaj Special School, South Goa. Mr. Shinde coached the Indian floor hockey team to four Gold Medals and one Bronze at the 2017 Special Olympics World Winter Games. He served as a Bocce Sports Presenter at the 2023 World Games and has mentored 14 international-level athletes who secured 13 medals for India.

Among the higher education faculty members receiving awards is Kirti Chandra Sahu from the Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad, whose pioneering research on the shape and size distributions of raindrops at different altitudes contributes to more accurate rainfall prediction. “He has developed a unique experimental facility from scratch that simulates atmospheric conditions experienced by raindrops as they descend from clouds to the ground, with potential applications in weather forecasting and climate modelling,” a spokesperson from the Union Ministry of Education said.

Another awardee, Avlokita Agrawal of IIT Roorkee, is a proponent of Vaastu Shastraand ‘Indian Knowledge System in Architecture’ through rational and scientific studies.

Vinay Chamola at the Birla Institute of Technology, Pilani, is receiving the award for the courses he has developed in the Internet of Things (IoT) and drone technology, and for establishing a hands-on IoT Tinkering Lab, translating cutting-edge research into project-based learning. “He also leads an interdisciplinary Shrimad Bhagavad Gita course that has demonstrably enhanced student well-being, blending technical excellence with compassion, values and purpose,” the spokesperson said.

Ankuran Dutta, Head of the Department of Communications, Gauhati University, who has founded Northeast India’s first community and web radio stations, is being awarded for his contribution to participatory communication and cultural outreach.

Another awardee, Shivani V., a faculty member at the Karnataka Sanskrit University, Bengaluru is being felicitated for her work in bridging traditional Sanskrit scholarship with Computational Linguistics, Artificial Intelligence, Digital Humanities, and Indian Knowledge Systems.

“Her research on a computational model for the linguistic study of Sanskrit reflects her pioneering efforts to connect Paninian grammar with modern language technology. She has contributed to major academic and technological initiatives, including Mahakosha, National Language Translation Mission, Shastrakosha, Pythonskrit, and Academic GPS, advancing the digitisation and computational study of Sanskrit knowledge,” the Education Ministry spokesperson stated.

World.title: Dairy conclave in Jhansi on September 11 as U.P. pushes women participation in rural economy
World.content:
Uttar Pradesh government on Friday said Dairy conclave of three divisions Jhansi, Chitrakoot and Kanpur will be held at Jhansi on 11th September, 2026, the theme of the conclave will be women participation & entrepreneurship in dairy development and contribution in dairy economy.

The Dairy Department said the objective of the conclave is to disseminate the advantages of various public welfare initiatives to eligible beneficiaries and promote rural economy.

“Dairy Development Department completed its 50 years on 17th April 2026. To commemorate this, under the blessings & guidance of Hon’ble CM Adityanath Yogi ji, a two-day Dugdamrit Swarn Mahotsav was organised in Lucknow, where thousands of milk farmers, investors, experts, technicians, academicians, milk-producing companies, SHGs, and co-operatives assembled. Shared their experiences on a single platform. Backwards and forward linkages were connected. Mahotsav also witnessed a dairy expo which showcased the strength of the dairy sector in Uttar Pradesh. Several government, non-government, and private stakeholders participated in the expo. The next dairy conclave is regionalised & focused for Bundelkhand & will be organised at Jhansi,” said Dhanalakshmi K., Dairy Commissioner, Uttar Pradesh, to The Hindu, in Lucknow.

“In the dairy sector, Bundelkhand is categorically known for its major women's involvement & participation in cooperatives & milk producing companies. The upcoming Dairy conclave in Jhansi aims to encourage & disseminate the advantages of various public welfare initiatives being executed by the Dairy Development Department to eligible beneficiaries. We aim to enhance awareness regarding modern technologies and scientific livestock management, quality control, and enhancement of value addition of the dairy products, while ensuring the effective execution of departmental schemes,” she added.

Speaking about the theme of the conclave, which will be women's empowerment and involvement of women in Dairy Development, Ms. Dhanalakshmi, the 2000-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer from the Uttar Pradesh cadre, added, “women by birth are better managers in the household. Dairy was not separate from domestic functions. It was part and parcel of domestic functions, which were run and managed by women. They were not only the caretakers of the family members but also of the domestic livestock which were integral part of the family.”

“The rearing and nurturing of the cows and other livestock was part of their life. They ran daily dairy farming activities like cleaning, fodder management, health care etc. They became contributors to family income, which became the force driving rural livelihood. They also ensured family nutrition as well as food security. Women as a whole emerged as major contributors in the dairy sector in India especially in Uttar Pradesh,” she added.

“Thus, women became a major part of our dairy cooperative sector more than 70%. Bundelkhand region, once was the drought prone dry region, has emerged as a dairy hub. In this region, women have taken active participation & 100% women owned & run co-operatives & milk producing companies have been formed. In Uttar Pradesh, 9 MPCs as of date are run & owned by women, which led to white revolution & complete change in the rural economy, nutrition & food security. Women who once were participants in dairy farming have become women entrepreneurs in the dairy sector. A large number of women are becoming Lakhpati Didis, who are the motivation for other women. They have not only strengthened their livelihood but also enhanced the GDP by contributing to the nation’s economy. Not far are the days when these women will become Crorepati Didis. Last but not least, these women's groups are entering into the dairy processing industry & eying on the domestic & international markets to provide quality nutritious milk & milk products,” she said.

“Hon’ble CM Sri Yogi Adityanath has encouraged & supported women dairy farmers & entrepreneurs. Nand Baba Dugd Mission has earmarked a minimum of 50% of the beneficiaries to be women in their schemes of Mukhyamantri Gosamvardhan Yojana, Mini Nandini, Nandini Krishi Samriddhi Yojana, as well as Pragatisheel Kisan Yojana. Uttar Pradesh Dairy Development & Milk Products Promotion Policy 2022 is also prioritising women entrepreneurs for subsidies of establishing dairy processing units,” she added.

World.title: Distrusting a system is not a problem at all, it is a sure sign of democratic progress: Former Orissa HC Chief Justice S. Muralidhar
World.content:
Former Chief Justice of the Orissa High Court S. Muralidhar, who chairs the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, speaks to Sarath Babu George about international humanitarian law, India’s position on Palestine, the ability of international institutions to hold powerful States accountable, judicial independence, constitutional offices, civil liberties and the Gen Z protests.

India has historically supported the Palestinian cause while maintaining strategic relations with Israel. From the standpoint of international law, how should India navigate this relationship? India will have its own compulsions. But there is a bottom line that we should never allow to be crossed. Here, the bottom line is international humanitarian law. We should not be among those countries that find it acceptable that children are dying of starvation or that children are dying for want of medical aid. I don’t think India is that kind of a country. It has never held itself out to be that kind of a country. If it is supporting the Palestinian cause, it should be deeply distressed by what is happening. And when it negotiates with Israel, it should place this at the forefront, express its disapproval of such actions, and take it from there.

Do you think international institutions such as the International Criminal Court are still capable of restraining powerful States when geopolitical interests run strongly in the opposite direction? The International Criminal Court is under a great deal of stress and pressure because sanctions have been imposed by the United States on its judges. This is very, very unfortunate. The rest of the world community, apart from making token protests, is doing very little about it. That is not a good sign. We expect all these international adjudicative bodies to be truly independent and free of political pressure. One hopes that this will change. We want all these systems to work. It is in the interest of countries such as India, countries in Africa and countries in South America, which are under tremendous geopolitical pressure, to have a mechanism where we can ask for answers. We must be able to hold governments and individuals within those governments accountable. There must be some forum where that can be done. So, it is very important, in the interest of all nations, that these mechanisms, whether the International Court of Justice or the International Criminal Court, are allowed to work fearlessly and truly independently.

Do you think the Indian judiciary today enjoys the level of institutional trust that it did a decade ago? What, in your view, has changed? I don’t think there has been a shift in the overall level of trust in the judiciary. Perhaps the judiciary has not always been able to meet the expectations that people have of it at different points in time. But there are also moments when it gives people hope. So, I would call it a mixed record; it is not a consistent one. People continue to come to the courts. There is also an element of choicelessness in coming to the courts. When you criminalise more and more ordinary activities, such as protests, people are bound to face the coercive element of the law and are forced to go to court. So, filings have gone up. If you go merely by the number of cases being filed, you cannot say that people have lost faith in the judiciary.

Q: There has, however, been growing apprehension about the independence of the courts -- from judicial appointments to the manner in which governments respond to judgments. What are the most serious institutional pressures facing the judiciary today? We have to look at the judiciary at three levels. I invariably emphasise that the district judiciary is far less independent than perhaps the High Courts or the Supreme Court ought to be. The extent to which individual judges succumb to pressure varies greatly. There are judges at all levels - the district judiciary, the High Courts and the Supreme Court - who have shown a remarkable degree of independence. But those judges are fewer in number than we would like them to be. That is what invites the comment that perhaps the judiciary is not as independent as it should be. I think the judiciary should be more assertive when it chooses people to be appointed to the High Courts and the Supreme Court and should not succumb to pressure at that stage. Secondly, it should take up cases involving government action in good time. It took four years to decide whether the conversion of a State into a Union Territory was legally valid. It took six years to decide whether demonetisation was legally valid. You cannot afford to take that long over electoral bonds. You allow so many elections to take place and then finally decide that the scheme was completely illegal. But then you allow the very party that collected the maximum funds to retain them. Somewhere, all of this is disappointing. It also raises questions about how independent and responsive the judiciary ought to be. So, again, it is not a consistent track record. I would say the hope is that it will become more independent.

Of late, we have witnessed a series of tussles between State governments and Governors. Does the constitutional design give Governors too much discretionary space, or is the problem primarily that constitutional conventions are not being respected? I don’t think either explanation is entirely true. You should see Governors for what they are. Whether it was under the earlier dispensation or the present one, Governors have acted according to the dictates of the Union Home Ministry. It has always been like that, and it continues to be like that. The office of the Governor has always been misused to invite someone to form a government or to dismiss a democratically elected government. That misuse continues. After the S.R. Bommai judgment, the imposition of President’s Rule has come down. But the misuse of the Governor’s office continues. I don’t think the Constitution envisaged the Governor as someone who was meant to exercise independent discretion in this manner. The office has effectively functioned as an extended arm of the Central government. And I want to emphasise that this is not peculiar to the present dispensation.

The use of investigative agencies has generated allegations of selective or politically motivated prosecution. What safeguards should the judiciary insist upon when the State invokes coercive powers? Criminal law is tested by procedure. There should be no dilution of procedural safeguards, such as furnishing the grounds of arrest. Whatever the coercive process, you cannot say that the requirement to furnish the grounds of arrest applies only under the regular criminal statutes and not under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act or some other law that also permits search, seizure and arrest. We must use the Constitution to say that, under any law, no arrest should take place without furnishing the grounds of arrest. When someone complains that the grounds were not furnished, you cannot say that the case has already progressed to the investigation stage and that it is too late to complain about the arrest. We must place the liberty of the individual at the highest value and be completely intolerant of any attempt to bypass procedure. Procedure is what tests criminal law and the actions of the State under criminal law. That is the most precious liberty a person has, and the courts have to stand very firm on this.

In this regard, how do you view the recent actions of the Enforcement Directorate across the country? There are judges in the Supreme Court who have told the Enforcement Directorate what it should and should not do. When the court tells it what it should not do, the Enforcement Directorate must respect that. The courts should be able to pull up the agency at every level. You should not have to go to the Supreme Court every time to establish that an action by the Enforcement Directorate is wrong. You should be able to go even to the court of first instance and say: don’t mechanically remand this person to the Enforcement Directorate's custody or judicial custody. Insist that the procedure is followed. The day that happens across the judicial hierarchy, citizens will have greater assurance that their liberties are secure.

We have also seen the emergence of Gen Z protests, with young people expressing distrust of institutions over examinations, jobs and questions of fairness. Is the problem that young people are becoming too distrustful of the system, or has the system given them too many reasons to distrust it? No. Distrusting a system is not a problem at all. It is a sure sign of democratic progress. We want our systems to function for the people. It is government by the people, for the people and of the people. Ultimately, governments are answerable to the people. Here, the people happened to be Gen Z, and they were doing a very basic exercise in democracy: asking for accountability in the exercise of power. They were making a simple statement: “We have entrusted you with certain powers, which have to be exercised for our benefit. Are you doing it or are you not? We believe you have not been doing it. We want you to answer for it.” They were exercising freedom of speech, freedom to form associations and the freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms and to express their voice. If you look at Article 19, I think Gen Z was exercising Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 19(1)(c) very systematically. And they were doing it with a wonderful sense of humour. There was also fearlessness. These are all healthy signs in a democracy.

World.title: 1,000 transplants and new beginnings: Thalassemia patients get a second chance
World.content:
When Muhammad Shaheem, 17, from Karnataka was diagnosed with severe thalassemia at just five months old, regular blood transfusions became a part of his childhood. Years of transfusions, however, led to severe iron overload that affected his heart and liver, making a stem cell transplant a particularly high-risk procedure.

A possible way out came from within his own family when Shaheem’s younger sister, Zara, 7, was identified as a full Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-matched donor. After extensive preparation and counselling at the Sankalp-Bhagwan Mahavir Jain Hospital in Bengaluru, his family decided to proceed with the transplant.

Their mother, Zareena, who lives with thalassemia major, said, “I continue to undergo treatment and regular blood transfusions. Though it was a difficult decision to make in my son’s case, it has ultimately given my son a second chance for better life without being troubled much by the disease.”

Mr. Shaheem is among 1,000 children who have undergone paediatric stem cell transplants with help from Sankalp India Foundation, DKMS, and Cure2Children. The procedure is both risky and expensive, and the treatment cost in India ranges from ₹12 lakh to ₹40 lakh.

On Friday (September 4), Sankalp, along with international nonprofit organisation DKMS and medical partner Cure2Children Foundation, completed 1,000 stem cell transplants for children suffering from thalassemia.

Of these transplants, DKMS has supported the transplantation costs of more than 820 children. On the other hand, Sankalp currently provides care to more than 3,000 children through 30 thalassemia day-care centres and operates paediatric bone marrow transplant centres in Bengaluru and Ahmedabad.

Rajat Kumar Agarwal, president of Sankalp India Foundation, said, “For us, these 1,000 transplants are 1,000 beginnings and proof that cure can be made accessible when organisations combine their strengths with a shared purpose. It shows how centres in resource-constrained settings can still achieve success in medicine and internationally recognised quality while keeping transplantation affordable and accessible.”

World.title: Swine flu cases surge to 441 in Mumbai
World.content:
Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.

According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.

To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.

The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’

Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.

Decline in monsoon related illnesses.

Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.

Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

World.title: Maharashtra Bill does not regulate private hospital treatment rates, says health right group
World.content:
Maharashtra Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill (CEB) has no provision to regulate treatment rates charged by private hospitals to patients, highlighted Jan Arogya Abhiyan (JAA), a coalition of NGOs and health professionals, on Friday while launching a statewide campaign appealing public to send objections to Joint Legislative Committee (JLC).

JLC is a committee comprising 21 MLAs, who have been reviewing the objections and suggestions on the Bill. The campaign also includes meetings with all 21 MLAs who are members of the JLC, demanding Health Minister convene a statewide consultation with organisations and networks working in the health sector to discuss the Bill.

JAA pointed out that the Bill must include fixed treatment charges for common procedures, different categories of beds, investigations, ICU services and doctors’ consultations; hospitals violating these rates should face penalties, a refund provision, a mandatory estimated bill by hospital detailing the treatment cost to be given to the patient, and the prescribed limit should not exceed estimated limit more than 5–10%.

The other suggested provision includes, ban withholding of patients or dead bodies over payment issues, establish accessible grievance-redressal system, establish an independent, well staffed regulatory authority, and ensure participation of all stakeholders in the State Council.

CEB was introduced in state Assembly on July 3, advocating compulsory registration of hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic centres transparency in treatment prices, and no deposit mandate for emergency cases. The new bill replaces the 77-years-old Maharashtra Nursing Homes Registration Act, 1949.

According to Arogya Abhiyan representatives, the analysis of hospital data from five major private hospitals in Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur shows that the average treatment charges faced by patients in these hospitals range from ₹24,000 to ₹62,000 per day. “This means just one day’s treatment in a large private hospital can cost as much as the average monthly per-capita income of a person in state,” said Abhay Shukla, the public health expert.

The latest NSS 80th Round data for Maharashtra shows as many as 77% of all hospitalisations in Maharashtra take place in private hospitals, highest among all states in India, average out-of-pocket expenditure on hospitalisation is ₹40,500, and on average rural hospitalisation costs have increased by 87%. 40 lakh people in Maharashtra are estimated to be pushed into poverty because of healthcare expenses.

Jan Arogya Abhiyan appealed to the Joint Legislative Committee to substantially strengthen this Bill in public interest as Section 11-Q of the Maharashtra Nursing Home Registration Act Rules, 2021 states that treatments rates should not exceed rates determined by the government.

World.title: Indian researchers map colonial spider’s venom gland, uncover molecules with potential for future cancer and antimicrobial drug research
World.content:
A team of Indian researchers has produced the first comprehensive molecular and functional profile of the venom gland of Stegodyphus sarasinorum, a colonial spider species found across the Indian subcontinent, to identify numerous proteins and small molecules that could serve as promising leads for future drug discovery.

Published in Springer Nature’s peer-reviewed, open-access journal Scientific Reports, the study identifies bioactive compounds associated with anti-cancer, antimicrobial and immune-related functions, while also demonstrating that venom gland extracts can kill cancer cells under laboratory conditions.

The researchers caution, however, that the findings represent an early stage of biomedical research and require extensive validation before any clinical application becomes possible.

Lead researcher A.P. Ajay Kumar of the Department of Zoology at Sree Neelakanta Government Sanskrit College, Pattambi, led the multidisciplinary study.

Unlike most spiders, which are solitary hunters, S. sarasinorum lives in permanent colonies, constructs communal silk nests and captures prey cooperatively. It is among only a small number of permanently social spider species known worldwide, thereby making it an important model for studying both spider behaviour and venom biology.

Although spider venom has long attracted scientific interest for their diverse biological activities, this is the first study to comprehensively analyse the molecular composition of the venom gland of this species using an integrated multi-omics approach, the researchers emphasise.

The research team combined transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy to examine the spider’s venom gland in great detail. Their analysis identified 31 protein components through transcriptomic profiling and 32 proteins through proteomic analysis. In addition, Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) detected 81 metabolites, including amino acids, biogenic amines and organic acids to provide a detailed molecular inventory of the venom gland.

To investigate the biological activity of these molecules, the researchers tested venom gland extracts against Dalton’s Lymphoma Ascites (DLA) cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The extracts exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, meaning that higher concentrations destroyed a greater proportion of cancer cells.

The findings suggest that the venom gland contains molecules with anti-cancer potential, the experiments were conducted only in cultured cells. Nonetheless, further studies involving additional cancer models, healthy cells, animals and eventually clinical trials will be required before any therapeutic use can be considered.

Among the most significant discoveries was the identification of several protein families that are already known for their biomedical relevance. These include hemocyanin proteins, which are known to stimulate immune responses and have attracted considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy research. The study also detected U12 and U20 lycotoxins, peptide molecules that can disrupt the membranes of bacteria and cancer cells, making them promising templates for the future development of antimicrobial peptides and targeted anti-cancer compounds.

The experimental work was carried out by research scholar Veena Venugopal, with contributions from collaborators from Calicut University, S.N. College, Nattika, St. Joseph’s College, Devagiri, PSG Institute of Advanced Studies, Coimbatore; GITAM University, Andhra Pradesh; and Ajman University, UAE.

World.title: PPP questions PM Shehbaz’s silence on new provinces
World.content:
• Nayyar Bokhari insists constitutional procedure, provincial consent are essential

• Rana Sanaullah says no such bill, resolution or preparations currently underway

ISLAMABAD: The PPP, a key ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition, has questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence over the debate on creating new provinces and sought his stance on the matter.

The PPP had earlier maintained that any move to create additional federating units must follow the procedure laid down in the Constitution. However, the PPP-led Sindh government on Wednesday got a resolution passed by the provincial assembly opposing any further division of the country’s existing four provinces.

Meanwhile, PML-N leader and Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Friday reiterated that no preparations were currently under way for the creation of new provinces.

During parliamentary proceedings last month, PPP lawmaker Agha Rafi­ullah had called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to come to the National Assembly and give a policy statement on the issue of new provinces.

Talking to Dawn on Friday, PPP Parliamentarians Secretary General Nayyar Hussain Bokhari sought the prime minister’s position on the issue.

A debate over the creation of new federating units has continued for the past couple of months in different circles, although there has been no official confirmation about the origin or contours of any proposal. However, some ruling-party leaders and federal cabinet members have publicly expressed support for the idea at different forums, including parliament.

Media reports have suggested proposals ranging from eight to as many as 30 provinces, though no official plan has been announced.

“We want to know what the stance of the prime minister on new provinces is, as no statement is coming from him, whereas a number of federal cabinet members are apparently supporting the plan,” Mr Bokhari said.

“It is a very serious issue which has jolted the existing federating units, but the PM is silent on such an important issue,” he added.

Mr Bokhari said that if the government was serious about increasing the number of provinces, it should first bring the matter before the federal cabinet, after which the prime minister should take all stakeholders and political parties on board.

He recalled that consultations between the government and political parties had continued for months during the framing of the 1973 Cons­titution, while deliberations preceding the 18th Constitutional Amendment had lasted for more than a year.

Mr Bokhari, who also raised the issue during a talk show on DawnNewsTV on Friday, said the consent of the provinces was essential for carving out new federating units. He said any such move would also require the necessary constitutional amendment to be passed by both the National Assembly and Senate with a two-thirds majority.

The PML-N-led government enjoys a two-thirds majority in the National Asse­mbly with the PPP’s support. Therefore, if the PPP pulled back its support, it would become impossible for the government to implement the idea.

Responding to a question about the local government system in the country, Mr Bokhari said any move in that regard must also follow the Constitution, particularly Article 140-A, which provides for the establishment of local governments by the provinces.

Meanwhile, Mr Sanaullah told a private television channel that no bill or resolution regarding the creation of new provinces had been presented in parliament.

He said consultation and consensus among political parties would be essential before any such bill or resolution could be brought before parliament.

Responding to a question, he said there was currently no discussion under way regarding the division of the existing provinces.

Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

World.title: War has made Tehran more confident, say US intelligence agencies
World.content:
WASHINGTON: Intelli­gence agencies in the United States believe that six months of war may have made Iran more, not less, confident in its ability to withstand American pressure and continue the conflict.

A New York Times report, published on Friday, says “Iran has grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East and appears determined to continue the conflict for months to frustrate the United States”.

The assessment comes as clashes resumed this week.

“The new exchanges have been limited so far. But the intelligence reports, according to people who have read them, suggest that Iran’s hardline government might be contemplating a significant escalation,” the newspaper reported.

The intelligence assessments also indicate that reaching an agreement to end the war could prove difficult. Current and former US officials told the NYT that there are few indications Tehran is ready to make a deal with Washington.

Mid-term elections

Some officials believe Tehran may seek to prolong the conflict until at least the US mid-term elections in November, calculating that continued warfare and high energy prices could create difficulties for President Trump and Republicans.

The report notes Donald Trump is currently not pursuing negotiations as he believes that economic pressure can force Tehran to make concessions concerning its control of the Strait of Hormuz and, eventually, its nuclear programme. But officials familiar with the intelligence told the NYT that sanctions could provoke further escalation.

Missile and drone capability

Iran’s military calculations appear shaped by its growing missile and drone capability and by its understanding of how to use the Strait of Hormuz as leverage. The strait carried roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war.

Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat and member of the House Intelligence Committee, described the Iranian leadership as increasingly confident. “Iranians are feeling pretty bullish about their position,” he said.

But at the same time he acknowledged that Iran has suffered substantial damage.

Other officials briefed on the intelligence said Iran may also believe that the United States will be constrained in launching major new attacks as its ammunition stocks decline.

Representative Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat and Intelligence Committee member, said: “The Iranians think they have maximum leverage.”

He suggested that, from Tehran’s perspective, continuing to pressure the Trump administration could serve its interests.

The conflict has also opened a cyber front. According to the Times, US officials believe Iran-linked hackers were probably responsible for attacks on more than 100 American water systems in late July. The attacks did not appear to make drinking water unsafe, although some caused disruptions requiring manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories.

Officials said Iranian hackers have also shown interest in US oil and gas infrastructure.

The New York Times reported that Iranian-linked cyber hackers may have regrouped after suffering losses early in the war. Former intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts said such attacks could remain attractive to Tehran because even limited disruptions might weaken American public support for a conflict with no clear end.

Alex Orleans, a former US government cybersecurity contractor who tracks Iranian hacking groups, said Iran’s cyberoperators probably feel emboldened. He warned that even unsuccessful attacks could serve a broader purpose by exhausting public patience with the conflict.

Influencing political scene

The report also describes Iranian efforts to influence US politics, including propaganda and social-media activity focused on mid-term elections. Meta recently identified a small network of Iran-based accounts on Facebook and Instagram that posted material concerning US politics.

Taken together, the intelligence assessments present a picture of an Iranian government that has been damaged but does not regard itself as defeated. Six months of warfare may have strengthened Tehran’s belief that it can absorb punishment, retain important military capabilities and continue imposing costs on the United States and its allies.

World.title: Maj Gen Faisal Naseer to head Nacta
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: In a significant development for Pakistan’s counter-terrorism framework, a key official of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Major General Faisal Naseer, has been appointed nati­onal coordinator of the National Counter Terro­rism Authority (Nacta).

According to a notification issued by the establishment division on Fri­day, Maj Gen Naseer’s, HI(M), T. Bt & Bar, appoi­ntment was made with the approval of the federal government.

He will serve as national coordinator, Nacta, under Section 9(1) of the Nacta Act, 2013, on a secondment basis.

The appointment is for a period of three years and is effective immediately, with standard terms and conditions and until further orders.

According to an Esta­bli­shment Division official, the transfer of a civi­lian offi­cer is made through dep­u­­tation, while serving army officers are posted from one organisation to an­o­ther on a secondment basis.

Commenting on the decision, a senior official within Nacta said there had been a proposal that the counter-terrorism authority should be run by a seasoned army or intelligence official. The move appears to be aimed at bringing greater strategic and operational experience to the authority, which has faced challenges in the past.

The official noted that the authority had previously operated without a proper strategy.

The appointment comes at a critical time for Nacta, which has historically struggled to function effectively as the country’s lead civilian counter-terrorism authority.

Despite being envisioned as a “one-window operation” to coordinate national counter-terrorism efforts, the agency has often been sidelined. In practice, the authority never fully evolved into the command and coordination body envisaged under the law, and has largely remained a policy secretariat with limited capacity to enforce decisions across the country’s sprawling security and law enforcement apparatus.

Initiatives taken over the last decade, including the establishment of the National Intelligence Fusion and Threat Asse­ssment Centre (NIFTAC) under Nacta, have raised concerns about centralisation and the weakening of democratic oversight.

The authority has also seen frequent changes at the top, with more than a dozen National Coord­inators since its inception, most of them drawn from the police service.

The appointment of Maj Gen Naseer, therefore, marks a departure from the usual practice. He had been serving as DG (counter-intelligence) since 2022, shortly after his promotion to the rank of major general.

The DG (C) post is often mistakenly described as heading the ISI’s counter-intelligence wing. However, the officer actually heads the agency’s Internal Wing, which deals with domestic security and political matters and, because of the nature of the assignment, frequently engages with the country’s principal power centres.

In the military’s conventional career progression, an officer moved out of an active military assignment is generally considered to have diminished prospects for further promotion, although exceptions have occurred.

Maj Gen Naseer’s transfer to Nacta has, consequently, left many observers surprised.

World.title: Govt reduces petrol price by Rs3.13, increases HSD by Rs3.74
World.content:
The government on Friday reduced the price of petrol by Rs3.13 per litre while increasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.74 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs345.87 per litre while HSD will cost Rs378.05 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will remain in effect from Sept 5 (Saturday) to Sept 7 (Monday).

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: 4 abducted Chinese nationals rescued in Islamabad
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The capital police recovered four Chinese nationals kidnapped for ransom after an encounter with a gang of criminals.

Earlier, the suspect was arrested in connection with a case registered at Shalimar Police Station and was being interrogated by the robbery and dacoity unit of the capital police.

During interrogation, the suspect disclosed that he, along with his accomplices, kidnapped the four Chinese nationals from F-10/4 for ransom. After the kidnapping, the victims were shifted to Bangial area and detained at a dairy farm. The suspect further disclosed that bargaining was in progress over the ransom for the release of the Chinese nationals. The suspect also offered assistance in taking the police to the farm.

A police team was constituted for the raid, and after reaching the area, the team cordoned off the farm. However, the suspect present inside the farm started indiscriminate firing at the police team, and as a result, panic spread in the area.

The police also retaliated and fired. Later, the police succeeded in capturing two kidnappers who were guarding the captives, detained in an adjacent room of the farm. The police found the four Chinese nationals in the room and took them into their safe custody.

Later, the raiding team arrested four more kidnappers and recovered weapons from them. However, the ringleader of the gang managed to escape from the spot.

Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

World.title: Nepra raises electricity costs by Rs2.58 per unit
World.content:
• Fuel adjustment adds Rs2.06 per unit to Sept bills

• 52 paisa per unit quarterly charge to continue through Nov; Rs45.6bn additional burden imposed on users

• Some relief for lifeline consumers, EV charging stations, prepaid users

ISLAMABAD: The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) on Friday notified about Rs46bn additional burden to electricity consumers by allowing Rs2.06 per unit higher fuel costs in July and about 52 paise per unit additional quarterly adjustment for other charges for next three months.

Consumers will bear the additional burden of about Rs3 per unit higher tariffs in September and then 52 paisa per unit for subsequent two months of October and November.

The impact of Fuel Cost Adjustment (FCA) alone in July works out at about Rs33bn and has mainly emanated from expensive LNG purchases from the spot market. Another Rs12.7bn Quarterly Tariff Adjustments (QTA) would be charged to consumers in three months.

In a late night notification, the Nepra said it “has decided that positive FCA for July 2026 i.e. Rs2.0581/kWh…shall be applicable to all the consumer categories of KE [K-Electric] and XWDISCOs except lifeline consumers, Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (EVCS) and prepaid electricity consumers, of all categories who opted for pre-paid tariff”.

The regulator, which has off late started issuing its decisions and notifications late in the night said the higher FCA would also be applicable to incremental consumption package consumers. Discos and KE are required to reflect the fuel charges adjustment in respect of July 2026 in the billing month of September 2026.

Concurrently, Nepra allowed a 52-paisa per unit higher quarterly tariff adjustment to be recovered over a period of three months.

“The positive quarterly adjustment of Rs0.5194/kWh shall also be billed to all the consumers (of Discos as well as KE) except lifeline, incremental consumption package billed units and prepaid consumers, to be passed in a period of 03 months i.e. September, October and November 2026”, the Nepra order said. This will be applicable at the uniform rate to all.

The decision to approve 52 paise will result in an overall positive adjustment of Rs12.67bn on account of variation in capacity charges, variable O&M, use of system charges, market operator fee, FCA impact on T&D losses and recovery of PPP on incremental units for year’s 2nd quarter.

The FCA is reviewed every month as per the tariff regime applicable across the country and is usually applicable to the consumer’s bills for one month only.

Under the tariff mechanism, changes in fuel cost are passed on to consumers only on monthly basis through automatic mechanism while quarterly tariff adjustments on account of variation in power purchase price, capacity cha­rges, variable operation and maintenance costs, use of system charges and including impact of transmission and distribution losses are built in the base tariff by the federal government.

Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

World.title: PPP blocks two gas revenue bills amid rift with govt
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Paki­s­tan Peoples Party on Friday blocked parliamentary proceedings on two government bills dealing with natural gas-related revenue adjustments amid the latest political bickering in the ruling coalition over recent elections in Azad Kashmir and discourse on the proposed creation of new provinces.

At a meeting of the National Assembly’s Stan­ding Committee on Petroleum, presided over by PPP’s Syed Mustafa Mehmood, lawmaker and former federal minister for petroleum and finance Syed Naveed Qamar asked the panel at the outset not to discuss the Natural Gas (Development Surcharge) Amendment Bill and the Gas Infrastructure Development Cess (GIDC) Amendment Bill.

NA body defers GIDC, gas development surcharge bills

The Petroleum Division had proposed the GIDC bill to expand the scope of GIDC funds’ utilisation for strategic oil and gas reserves from its existing specific mandate of developing Pakistan-Iran, Turkmenistan-Pakistan and cross-country gas pipelines. About Rs295 billion remains unutilised in the public kitty, while more than Rs400bn collected by fertiliser companies from consumers remains outside the national exchequer because of legal issues.

Outside the meeting, Mr Qamar told reporters that the PPP was not a coalition partner but had been supporting the government and that the relationship could not be carried forward unilaterally forever. He said his party had conveyed certain reservations to the government which, if it required PPP’s support, it had to resolve. These complaints related to AJK elections, appointment of judges and other matters.

He said the government had promised to look into those issues but had not shown any progress. Ther­efore, the PPP had decided that it would not support the government until tangible progress was seen.

He said the government had tried to bulldoze a bill through the interior panel a day earlier. He said the Islamabad Local Government Bill was unacceptable even otherwise and the PPP had filed a dissenting note. “The government needs to resolve these issues and take steps,” he said, adding that the law minister was abroad and it was unclear where he was active these days.

Committee Chairman Mustafa Mehmood said cheap gas should not be provided to fertiliser companies if the benefit did not reach the farmer. The committee then decided to defer both bills.

Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

World.title: Poor connectivity in GB hampers tourism, disaster response
World.content:
• Chief Minister Hussain says satellite connectivity essential to monitor 7,000 glaciers, protect region from catastrophe

• Senate committee directs measures to improve internet, oil and LPG supplies in the region

GILGIT: Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Minister Amjad Hussain informed a parliamentary committee on Friday the poor state of cellular connectivity in the region not only affected tourism but also severely hampered relief and rescue operations during emergencies.

Addressing a meeting of the Senate Standing Committee on Cabinet Secretariat, presided over by its chairman Senator Mahmood-ul-Hassan, at the GB Assembly in Gilgit, CM Hussain said satellite connectivity was essential for monitoring the 7,000 glaciers in GB and ensuring effective disaster management to protect the region from any major catastrophe.

He said the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) should play a proactive role in ensuring stable internet connectivity in GB. He clarified that the Special Com­munications Organisation (SCO) was merely a service provider and, therefore, the PTA should fulfil its responsibilities as the regulator.

He said fibre-optic connectivity was feasible only in the urban areas, while it was a limited option for other mountainous and difficult-to-access areas.

CM Hussain said satellite connectivity was essential for monitoring glaciers and keeping track of natural disasters in the region, citing the recent natural disaster in Nepal as an example of the importance of such connectivity. He added that effective disaster response was possible only through coordination among all relevant institutions.

PTA Chairman retired Gen Hafeezur Rehman told the committee that, in accordance with the directives of PM Shehbaz, the authority was taking measures to improve internet services in GB. He said obstacles and challenges affecting internet connectivity in the region would be reviewed and necessary steps would be taken to address them.

The committee chairman said GB was amo­ng the most beautiful regions in the world and attracted thousands of tourists every year, but slow internet speeds remained a major issue and required immediate attention. He said no country or region could develop in the modern era without reliable internet connectivity.

Therefore, Senator Hassan said, it was essential to provide the GB people with modern, high-speed and quality internet services. He said another meeting would be held in Gilgit, inviting all relevant stakeholders and private network companies to discuss improvements in internet services.

Senior officials of the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) briefed the committee on disaster preparedness, early warning systems, rescue facilities and available funds in GB. They also briefed the committee on the damage caused by floods, landslides, avalanches and other natural disasters during the past five years, compensation paid to victims, and relief and rescue operations.

The committee chairman stressed the need to further strengthen the role of the NDMA in dealing with natural disasters in GB. He said floods and other natural disasters had caused extensive damage in various parts of the reg­ion, making it essential to ensure the timely provision of assistance to affected communities.

Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) Chairman Nabeel Awan briefed the committee on the availability, transportation and storage of petroleum products and LPG in GB. He said the region had sufficient storage capacity to maintain oil reserves capable of meeting its requirements for 20 to 30 days. He also briefed the committee on oil storage facilities in Baltistan division.

Senator Aamir Waliuddin Chishti directed that oil and LPG storage capacity in GB be increased. He asked Ogra officials to effectively raise issues related to oil and LPG storage in GB with the federal petroleum ministry and take necessary measures for their permanent resolution.

Special Technology Zones Authority (STZA) Chairman Azfar Manzoor briefed the committee via video link on various issues concerning GB. He said the authority had previously taken steps towards establishing a special technology zone in the region and was ready to continue playing its role in this regard.

The body chairman said GB was a tax-free region and, therefore, there should be no technical difficulty in establishing a special technology zone in the region.
