World.title: Ambulance system incident not a failure, QAS says amid claims of late arrivals
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health Ambulance system incident not a failure, QAS says amid claims of late arrivals Dominique Tassell Updated September 5, 2026 — 3:28pm ,first published 2:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Ambulance Services have said it is inaccurate to describe this week’s incident as a system failure, as politicians continue to clash over its impacts. The QAS’ computer-aided dispatch (CAD) system was upgraded on Thursday, but resulted in staff having to manually relay important information to ambulances by radio. Health Minister Tim Nicholls. Courtney Kruk Triple Zero calls were not impacted and QAS said it has not received any reports of adverse impacts to patients from the transition. A QAS spokesperson said Queenslanders can be confident they will receive ambulance services if they call Triple Zero.



“Our systems are working as intended following the transition to our new CAD system,” they said. “All Triple Zero calls are being answered and resources are being dispatched in a timely manner, with the most urgent cases prioritised.” The possible impact on the system during the transition was anticipated and accounted for, the QAS spokesperson said. Loading “Business continuity processes were enacted during the transition … this included rostering additional staff and validating all incidents to ensure they received an appropriate response,” they said.



While there have been reports in the media of ambulances arriving significantly late or not arriving at all, health minister Tim Nicholls said this was completely untrue. “There was an alternative system in the event that the changeover didn’t go exactly according to plan,” Nicholls said. Nicholls said it was “absolutely disingenuous and really quite despicable” for the state opposition to claim services were impacted. “We’re not aware of any reports that anyone has made that they’ve had to drive themselves because they were unable to get through to Triple Zero,” he said. “Now, there might be people who called through and weren’t either a category one, two, or three. That might be the normal course of events, but certainly nothing as a result of the changeover in the system has led to that delay that I’m aware of.”



Nicholls said QAS staff are used to the manual system and it was regularly used during updates to the old system. However, the state opposition has maintained the incident was more serious than is being communicated, claiming that ambulances became stuck in a queue due to dispatch issues and could not reach people quickly. Opposition leader Steven Miles once again slammed the state government for the system failure on Saturday. Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the state government is not being truthful about a QAS systems incident on Thursday (file photo). William Davis “We’re calling for a full investigation, a full review of what went wrong with the systems upgrade, why they weren’t able to roll back to the legacy system that was stable and working, and what they will put in place to ensure that this never happens again,” Miles said.



“The people talking to us say that they have never experienced a shutdown of the dispatch system like what occurred this week. “[Premier] David Crisafulli once said that ambulances not arriving on time was incomprehensible in a modern Queensland, but it is precisely what we’ve seen this week under this. “And yet the government and the ambulance service seems determined to not tell Queenslanders how many people waited for an ambulance, how many people never had, how many people were so sick and in such pain that they drove themselves to hospital rather than wait for an ambulance that. “It’s about time the health minister came clean with Queenslanders about what really happened during the week with ambulance dispatches.” Nicholls labelled these comments appalling, and said he would not stand for the opposition labelling QAS liars.



“Labor’s shameful efforts to politicise this much-needed system upgrade shows just how little respect they have for our hardworking paramedics and QAS staff,” he said. “After a decade of decline, Labor left the QAS with outdated legacy systems that were not fit-for-purpose, following their decision to disband the Public Sector Business Agency.” On Saturday morning, Miles said Queenslanders are rightly very proud of our ambulance service. “Our Ambos do a fantastic job,” he said. “People come from around the world to see how the Queensland Ambulance Service operates, but we need to keep it that way.



“These kinds of rushed system upgrades that have caused the outage on Thursday will only cause Queenslanders to doubt the quality of their ambulance service.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
A Qantas flight has diverted to Christchurch shortly after take-off from Queenstown.

A witness told RNZ they were watching planes take off when they saw what they believed to be a "burst of flames" from the left engine.

They "then heard a series of loud bangs, like two or three".

"Quite the sight really," they said.

Christchurch Airport confirmed they were aware of an incident but could not confirm further details.

Queenstown Airport said flight QF122 was diverted to Christchurch soon after departure on Saturday afternoon.

RNZ understands flight QF122 was carrying 160 passengers.

Queenstown Airport remains operational.

Hato Hone St John said it was notified of a flight diversion at 4.25pm.

"Multiple ambulance resources have responded to Christchurch Airport as a standard procedure."

Fire and Emergency New Zealand have been contacted for more information.

Police said they had been notified, but officials were yet to reveal the nature of the problem.

World.title: Pedestrian hit by car in Gisborne
World.content:
A pedestrian has been seriously injured after being struck by a car in Gisborne on Saturday afternoon.

Police said it happened on Lytton Road in Te Hapara at about 3pm.

The road has been closed, with traffic diversions in place.

Motorists are advised to avoid the area and expect delays.

World.title: Sititi siblings set for special day as Black Ferns and All Blacks take on South Africa
World.content:
Wallace and Amarante Sititi will make their family incredibly proud this weekend when they both represent New Zealand on the world stage.

Both loose forwards, 19-year-old Amarante is in the reserves for the Black Ferns' historic match with the Springbok Women on Saturday night in Johannesburg before Wallace will come off the bench for the All Blacks in Sunday morning's crucial third test against the Springboks in the second game of the double header.

It's only the second time in history that siblings have represented New Zealand's men's and women's rugby teams on the same day, with Xavier and Annaleah Rush the first to achieve the feat in 1998.

Drama brewing around Black Ferns vs Springbok Women Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

"Obviously, it's special just to be in this All Blacks team, and to have my little sister here sitting next to me is definitely special. Doing it on the same day, and wearing the same number is crazy," Wallace said.

"I'm extremely proud. She's put in a lot of hard work to get here, and although it's been a quick rise to where she is at the moment, I think that's a testament to how hard she's worked and the time she's put into it."

All Black Wallace Sititi in action against the Lions, 2026. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Wallace said his sister has been talented from a young age.

"She played a lot of sports growing up. I think the last two years of school she really took it seriously, and I remember one conversation we had in the car ride home when I picked her up from school; she said she wanted to do this professionally, and I said if that's what you want, then stick to the lord and he'll guide you through it."

Teenager Amarante, who made her debut last month in New Zealand's big win over Australia, can't wait to get out on the field and said it was "surreal" being involved in the first Black Ferns game against the Springbok Women in South Africa.

She said playing on the same day as her older brother would be amazing.

"Representing this country is a privilege, but doing it alongside my brother is something special, and I'll always hold it in my heart. Just like Wally said, it's all because of our family and their prayers," Amarante said.

"I'm still buzzing that I get to be here with my brother. I don't think I've told him yet, but he's a big inspiration for me, just like my dad."

Black Ferns on debut Amarante Sititi, Elinor-Plum King and Shyrah Tuliau-Tua’a - The O’Reilly Cup - New Zealand Black Ferns v Australia Wallaroos at Go Media Stadium, Auckland, New Zealand. Saturday 22 August 2026 the © Photo: Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz Brett Phibbs

The pair are the children of former Samoa loose forward and captain Semo Sititi, who played 59 tests for Samoa between 1999 and 2009.

Semo arrived in Johannesburg last night and will be on hand to watch his children at Soweto's FNB Stadium, where about 90,000 fans are expected.

"It wasn't planned that he was going to be here," Wallace said.

"We sort of had this date in the back of our minds, that there was a possibility it could happen. And then, when we found out earlier in the week that we were both going to play, he said he would somehow make his way here.

"He's had a massive influence on us, not only as rugby players, but as people. And our mother, who unfortunately can't be here."

The siblings had dinner with their dad last night, and he imparted some familiar fatherly advice.

"He said just to play my game and just be myself," said Amarante.

"That's his advice to me every game, to be myself and not be pressured by any outside noise."

World.title: League fans fuming after Sky cuts to betting ad as Jai Arrow walks out for 100th game
World.content:
A Sky sport boss has apologised after the network cut their feed to a betting ad during an emotional walk onto the field for NRL Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow at his 100th game, as he retires with motor neurone disease.

The 31-year-old retired from rugby league earlier this year - just two games shy of his hundredth match - as he battles motor neurone disease.

Following his diagnosis, the NRL approved a special one-off rule change that would allow Arrow to reach the milestone with his former club; being named as an additional player on the team list and interchange rotation.

New Zealand audiences missed the emotional walk on as, instead, an ad for Betcha began to roll.

Their screens returned to the pitch right on the kick-off whistle.

Sky sport content head Gary Burchett told Newstalk ZB the cut away to an advert was not automated, and was made by their crew who were working on the broadcast live: "We got this badly wrong last night and we're deeply sorry."

Customer feedback had been "colourful and upset, and at points downright disgusted", and the team would review what led to the decision, and the editorial process for the future, he said.

"We knew the significance of Jai's walkout, and we knew what that moment was to Jai and his family and his teammates and fans at he NRL. And simply, we should have shown that moment in full, live. That's the obligation that we have to our customers and to fans of rugby league.

"And I'm also very conscious for those people and their families who face the daily realities and challenges of motor neurone disease, because that story resonates and goes well beyond the code itself, right. So we let them down too."

Another NRL match feed had run late on the broadcast, Burchett told ZB, which created an unintended "scheduling error" as the crew tried to fit the ad in before kick-off: "We missed an incredibly important moment ... our job is to recognise the moments that matter... this was unquestionably one of those moments, and we missed it, and it hurts."

Livid fans posted on social media, calling the move "unbelieveable", "disgusting" and "disrespectful".

"My wife died of motor neurone disease and tonight I sat with my two children to watch Jai Arrow in his 100th game walking on to the field. This was suppose to be a special moment to remember my wife and their mum, but we had to watch a betting advert. I am hopeful that Sky tv issues an apology to Jai Arrow and MND New Zealand, and to my devastated children. I am so very disappointed," one person wrote.

Others threatened to cancel their subscriptions to Sky and their Betcha accounts.

Sky earlier issued a statement, saying the ad break was due to a scheduling error: "To ensure fans can enjoy the moment as it happened, we have shared the full celebration across our social media channels and will also make it available to watch on demand."

Comments on the post were turned off.

RNZ has also approached Betcha for comment.

Arrow's exemption saw him lead the Rabbitohs onto the field at Cbus Super Stadium for his 99th game last weekend, arm-in-arm with teammate Cody Walker, and greeted by a standing ovation.

He was then taken off three seconds after kick-off against the Gold Coast Titans - despite jokingly trying to wave off the call from Rabbitohs co-captain Cameron Murray. He was permitted to remain on the bench in his playing kit for the remainder of the match.

Jai Arrow (right) walks onto the field on 29 August, at this 99th match. Chris Hyde

Prior to the game, footage from the changing sheds showed veteran coach Wayne Bennett helping Arrow pull up his socks on and lace his boots.

Before medically retiring at the start of the year, Arrow played 178 NRL matches. His first-grade career started in 2016 with 24 games across two seasons for the Brisbane Broncos, followed by 56 games for the Gold Coast Titans, then finally 98 games for South Sydney from 2021 - 2025.

World.title: Rental with soggy floorboards and leaky roof among first to jump tribunal queue
World.content:
A Wellington family who slept in the lounge of their three-bedroom rental because of mould and a hole in the bedroom floor has found a new home, after their case was bumped up the tribunal queue.

With claims of soggy rotten floorboards, a leaking roof, and widespread mould, the case is one of the first to be part of the Tenancy Tribunal's pilot to prioritise severe health and safety cases.

The tribunal told RNZ it had assessed the matter as involving a potentially significant health and safety claim and scheduled an urgent case conference.

The first hearing was on 26 August, eight days after it was lodged - a much faster turnaround than the tribunal's 48-day average wait time last year.

As the claim was ongoing, the tribunal said it could not comment further on the case.

RNZ has seen emails between the family and property agency Quinovic, which manages the rental, in which requests for alternative accommodation were initially declined.

However, RNZ understands that this week Quinovic began working closely with the family to relocate them.

Brendon's son's bag grew significant mould after sitting on the floor for two weeks. Supplied

Brendon, who asked to go by his first name only, said he was paying $660 per week for the three-bedroom home that was "borderline ready to be condemned".

He lived at the home with his 6-year-old son, and the child's mother, who gave birth to their second child last week.

When the family moved into the home in June, Brendon said they were told it was Healthy Home-certified.

"I got sick at least twice in the first month of trying to clean up all the mould and the rot."

And a medical certificate seen by RNZ said the then-pregnant woman needed immediate alternative accommodation, as the rental was making her sick.

Brendon said the largest bedroom was not being used, as it had a large hole in the floor covered by carpet.

"If you had jumped, you would have gone straight through it.

"I mean, it's clearly not livable."

The renter said the home had severe soggy floorboards and leaks. Supplied

Brendon said major repairs to the kitchen, which was rotting and mouldy, made it unusable for over a month.

The tribunal's three-month pilot, which began in August, is trialing prioritising cases with serious health and safety risks, like significant mould, structural issues, or methamphetamine contamination.

Rent arrears cases - when a tenant is behind on rent payments - are also being moved up the queue as part of the trial.

Emails seen by RNZ show Quinovic originally rejected Brendon's requests for rent reduction and alternative accommodation, with staff telling him to take his concerns to the tribunal if he wished.

One email reads: "With regard to your request for temporary accommodation, there is no general obligation under the Residential Tenancies Act for a landlord to provide or pay for alternative accommodation while repairs are being carried out. We do not currently have a suitable alternative property available in the area."

However, it was prepared to agree on an early tenancy termination date.

Quinovic originally rejected Brendon's requests for rent reduction and alternative accommodation. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Quinovic chief executive Parrish Wong later told RNZ it had been working with the family and supported them moving out of the property and into alternative accommodation.

"We will continue to work with the family and support them to help ensure the right accommodation moving forward."

Brendon said Wong had stepped in this week and was ensuring the family was assisted with moving belongings in and out of storage, and into a new home.

In March, the government announced proposals to develop a "light touch" approach to regulate property managers, including a register and separate disciplinary tribunal.

World.title: Māori Queen urges future generations to transform trauma into triumph
World.content:
"E kore teenei whakaoranga e huri ki tua o aaku mokopuna, ka puta, ka ora" - Kiingi Tawhiao.

Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po has called on Māori to change the trajectory for future generations, urging her people to move from the legacy of Raupatu to a future of Rauora.

In her second Koroneihana address, Te Arikinui told thousands who gathered at Tūrangawaewae Marae and beyond that the mauri of kotahitanga, carried and protected by her father, Kiingi Tuuheitia Potatau Te Wherowhero te tuawhitu, now rests with everyone.

Her use of the term Raupatu refers to the impact of colonisation and intergenerational trauma that has continued to trickle across te ao Māori. Rauora symbolises wellbeing, health and prosperity.

Te Arikinui delivered the kauwhau in te reo Māori, and the office of the Kiingitanga provided translations which reflected in English the sentiment she carried.

"We are descendants of Raupatu. But we must also become Toa o te Rauora," Te Arikinui said.

"Rauora is more than recovery. It is revival. It is the full expression of who we are and who we can become.

"It is our tamariki growing up strong in their reo, their whakapapa and their potential, knowing they can stand anywhere in the world without leaving behind who they are.

"It is our whānau healthy and secure. Our people owning homes, building wealth, creating businesses and institutions, growing leaders and determining our own future.

"It is our whenua and wai flourishing alongside us.

"And it is Māori looking beyond the challenges of today to the possibilities of tomorrow, leading in technology, innovation, enterprise, science, energy and industries yet to be imagined."

Te Arikinui drew on the words of her tūpuna Kiingi Tawhiao, asking what his hope that his mokopuna would prosper and thrive should look like today.

The Māori monarch, Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po. Image courtesy of Te Tari o te Kiingitanga

"Rauora is not simply having a place in the future. It is having the strength, confidence and imagination to shape it. A people alive with possibility. That is Rauora."

She said kotahitanga did not mean Māori would always agree, but meant being able to disagree without diminishing or dividing one another.

"Let us spend less of our strength fighting one another and more of it building what our people need."

Te Arikinui grew up in the shadow of Raupatu, as did many of her generation.

"Raupatu is part of our story. It must never become the limit of our story."

She said Māori would never forget what happened, but the burden of the past could not be allowed to determine how far future generations could go.

She questioned whether it was enough for some Māori to prosper while too many whānau continued to struggle with the basics.

"Surely our tūpuna wanted more for us than survival.

She challenged Māori to stop asking only what had happened to them, and instead ask what they would do now.

"The question for us is no longer only what happened to us; it is also: What will we do now? When do we decide that what we inherited will not be what we hand on?

"When do we say, 'The trajectory changes with us'?"

Tamariki bring their loved ones to Tūrangawaewae. Image courtesy of Te Tari o te Kiingitanga

Te Arikinui said the circumstances Māori were born into should not determine the limits of their lives.

"E ruhi mā, e koro mā, tamariki mā, mokopuna mā: Koinei te rā. This is the day. This is the day I say: Raupatu was part of the world I was born into, but Raupatu is not all that I am. I am an uri of Raupatu, but I will be a toa of Rauora. Ka puta. Ka ora," she said.

"I will not allow the circumstances into which I was born to determine the limits of my life. I will learn. I will work. I will lead. I will build. And I will leave something stronger for those who come after me. Koinei te rā.

"E koro, Raupatu, rest here. You have brought us this far. I will never forget you. There will be times when I reach for you again and draw strength from you. But today, let the burden fall from our shoulders."

Te Arikinui has urged Māori to look within their own whānau, and become living and breathing examples of health and wellbeing.

"Aku toa o te Rauora, now it is our turn. Maranga mai rā. Rise. Rise from poverty, from dependency, from the belief that somebody else must determine our future.

There will be successes. There will be setbacks. But we are not powerless. We are descendants of Raupatu. Now let us be champions of Rauora.

"The time has come for our pakeke to guide and strengthen a generation that is courageous, capable and ready. And the time has come to stop believing that our future sits entirely in the hands of government.

"Government has responsibilities. Those responsibilities must be honoured. But we also have responsibilities to ourselves and to those who come after us.

"We must build our own whare. Our reo, our taiao, our hauora and our pā harakeke are foundations for that future. Our Kotahitanga gives us the strength to build it together."

World.title: Blaze at cafe next to New Zealand's oldest building 'suspicious', FENZ says
World.content:
A café situated just metres from New Zealand's oldest surviving building has been damaged in an overnight blaze, but volunteer firefighters managed to stop the flames spreading to 204-year-old Kemp House at Kerikeri Basin.

Police are investigating the blaze, which started in a storage shed next to Honey House Café around 11.30pm on Friday.

The shed was destroyed while one wall of the café was burned and its water pipes and electric cables were badly damaged.

The two-storey Honey House has the café on the ground level and offices for Heritage New Zealand upstairs.

The business is next to Kemp House, which was built between 1821 and 1822 by missionaries, and was an important focus for early relationships between Māori and Pākehā.

Another heritage building, the Stone Store, which was built not much later - from 1832 to 1836 - is also next door to the cafe.

The fire had been small, and "both Kemp House and Stone Store were thankfully unaffected by the blaze," a Honey House Café spokesperson said.

The Stone Store and Kemp House, seen from Kororipo Pā in 2025. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Kerikeri deputy fire chief Andy Hamberger said the nation owed a debt of gratitude to a Kerikeri man whose vigilance may have saved New Zealand's oldest building.

Hamberger said a man on his way to work about 11.30pm on Friday called 111 when he spotted smoke near Kerikeri Basin.

The first fire truck at the scene found a storage shed next to the Honey House Café - which was immediately behind the 204-year-old Kemp House - was burning fiercely.

The crew called for a second truck as well as backup from Ōkaihau and Paihia.

Hamberger said the shed was razed and the café's exterior, water pipes and electrical cabling were badly damaged.

Kerikeri deputy fire chief Andy Hamberger during an exercise at the Stone Store in February this year. PETER DE GRAAF / RNZ

If firefighters had arrived a few minutes later the flames could have taken hold of the two-storey Honey House and spread from there to nearby Kemp House, which was currently wrapped in plastic for re-roofing.

"It was called in by a chap who was going to work, he spotted the fire," Hamberger said.

"Without him the potential for spread to Kemp House was actually quite scary, to be honest, because they've got it surrounded with plastic sheeting to protect it. Potentially we could have had a fire in that Kemp House as well," he said.

"I don't know him but a big shout out to that guy, because without him being pretty vigilant on his way to work, we could be looking at a major building fire, or a heritage building being lost, or certainly significantly damaged."

John O'Hare, Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga spokesman for Northland, said the entire Kerikeri Mission Station site was closed while police and FENZ carried out their investigations.

It was too early to say with certainty what had caused the fire but initial indications were that it had been deliberately lit.

Fortunately, neither Kemp House nor the Stone Store had been damaged.

"But it was too close for comfort. It was very, very close, and we're just very thankful that that Kemp House didn't catch alight, and incredibly disappointed that somebody would do this. The indicators are that this was a deliberate act, which is appalling," O'Hare said.

The café was likely to be closed for the foreseeable future.

The cause had yet to be confirmed but if police found it had been deliberately lit, as was suspected, that would be "appalling" and "deeply disappointing", he said.

Despite its historic appearance, the Honey House - a former curator's cottage - was only built in 1976.

It was built on the site of a historic barn and took its name from James Kemp Jr's storage shed for beehives, which once stood nearby.

The café opened in 2012 with some of its recipes sourced from historic archives, or made with fruit grown in Kerikeri Mission Station's heritage orchard.

Kemp House was erected in 1821-22 by the London-based Church Missionary Society for the Reverend John Butler, the only ordained minister in the settlement at the time.

It was built by missionary carpenters and Māori sawyers, and later became the home of the Kemp family.

Kemp House is currently wrapped in plastic [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regions/1079908/work-underway-on-roof-of-204-year-old-kemp-house-in-kerikeri while it is roof shingles are being replaced], which could have made a fire even more catastrophic.

World.title: The psychiatrist who can now prescribe MDMA
World.content:
Dr Gary Wynn is one of two psychiatrists who have just been approved to administer and prescribe MDMA in New Zealand, to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

In legal terms, MDMA is a Class B high risk drug. It is also known as ecstasy, E, or molly, and is a stimulant and hallucinogen.

It is the first time MDMA assisted treatment has been allowed in Aotearoa.

Dr Wynn talked with Saturday Morning about the research his team will be doing, who could be treated, and what their sessions might look like.

The Psychiatrist Who Can Now Prescribe MDMA Saturday Morning Download MP3 22m

In the 1970s, MDMA's first use was as a medicine known as 'empathy', used by therapists," Wynn says.

"It creates an openness, a connection. An empathy-enhancing compound that sort of reduces the fear centres in the brain, and puts people in this really open space to do some deep work, particularly around traumas that they've experienced in their life."

In the early 1980s MDMA became better known as a party drug, and by the mid-1980s it was made illegal in the United States - which soon became the norm around the world. "And we spent 40-ish years with it being illegal, until Australia in 2023."

Australia's medicines regulator granted permission in 2023 for psychedelics to be used in therapy nationally there, including psilocybin for depression, and MDMA for PTSD.

What could MDMA do clinically?

MDMA's potential "is pretty amazing," Wynn says.

He has done training in Canada and Australia on providing MDMA treatment, and will be working with Dr Tom Paterson for the New Zealand trials.

"It's one of those drugs that when it works it feels almost magical, people get better sometimes so quickly and so intensely that you're like 'wow', it's almost unbelievable given the typical history of psychiatric treatments where medications take months to work, therapies sometimes years to work.

"In one study, about 80 percent of people were significantly better from treatment from three rounds of MDMA treatment, and at least 50 percent had full remission of their PTSD. And I don't know anything else that even comes close to those numbers in terms of treatment efficacy for PTSD."

Who could receive the treatments?

"There's a lot of reasons people can be severely traumatised," Wynn says.

"Military and veteran PTSD had got a lot of attention - I think deservedly so - but the truth of the matter is people get traumatised and severely traumatised from a whole host of reasons." Among them, sexual assault, prolonged childhood abuse and domestic violence, he says.

The test patients will be people who have PTSD, and who have not had success with an earlier treatment, such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor medicines) or talk therapy.

"Typically we're looking at more severe cases upfront.

"That's the other really unique thing about MDMA, most treatments for PTSD as you get more severe the treatments work less and less, so they work the best in sort of mild to moderate PTSD. And then gosh, really severe PTSD, nothing seems to work."

But so far, MDMA trials seem to show pretty even benefit across the different severities of PTSD, he says.

What will the work involve?

MDMA affects a number of neurotransmitters in the brain, including serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine and oxytocin - a brain chemical involved with feelings of connection. It also quietens down the fearful side of the brain, Wynn says.

"So it's not just the connection, it's the connection and then this quieting down of the fearful parts of the brain. I think those two things work in tandem to put someone into this really open state where they can look at their traumas in a less overwhelmed way."

The protocol the team will use is a "fairly intense and fairly long protocol", he says. It is modelled off the earlier US FDA approved MAPS (Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies) clinical trial protocol.

First, prospective patients are screened with a full psychiatric examination and health screening. Then there will be rounds of treatment, which each consist of three stages - a preparation phase, a medicine session and an integration session.

"There's two therapists for all of this time - so the two therapists and the individual will get to know each other. You do need a lot of trust and understanding, a lot of rapport, a lot of understanding of what the shape of all their traumatic experiences are, understanding about their social supports.

"You need to understand the person pretty well, so that can take a lot of hours to get to that point."

They will then run a full day medicine session, during which the MDMA dose will be given, after "careful preparation to get them into a calm state".

"We administer the drug, it takes maybe half an hour to work, at which point they go into this altered state. Some people get pretty significantly into an altered state, some people have a sort of milder experience.

"Then during that time we do the therapeutic work looking at the traumas, processing things, somewhat allowing them to go where their mind wants to take them. There's a classic comment in psychedelics talking about the inner healing intelligence - that some of the job is getting out of the way and letting the mind do the work of healing itself."

It's a long day with a lot of emotions, he says: "pretty intense".

"Then after that completes, we'll do three or four more sessions with the two therapists and the individual where you're trying to integrate what happened, you're trying to make sense of it, you're trying to take these learnings from that day-long experience and action them into the real world."

With three rounds typical for each of the preparation phase, medicine session and integration sessions for each patient: "All told, there's about 50-ish hours of therapist time, and there's two therapists the entire time."

Wynn says people using MDMA recreationally are not guaranteed of the purity of what they're taking, whereas the MDMA used in this approved trial will be pharmaceutical grade and pure.

MDMD is also known as ecstasy, E or molly. Supplied/ NZ Drug Foundation

The Drug Foundation has warned that drugs illegally sold as MDMA in New Zealand can sometimes have other things mixed into them, or even be another substance altogether - in particular synthetic cathinones (often called bath salts): And that "these drugs can have more unpleasant and unpredictable effects than MDMA".

Wynn says he hopes their team will have their first patient receiving the treatment within the next two to three months.

World.title: Ben Simmons signs multi-million-dollar NBA deal with Kings
World.content:
Australian former number one overall draft pick Ben Simmons has taken a significant step towards resurrecting his NBA career, agreeing to a one-year deal with the Sacramento Kings.

The Melbourne-born guard returns on a $US3.5 million ($4.9 million) contract after sitting ‌out the entire 2025-26 campaign while rehabilitating back and leg injuries that have hampered him in recent years.

Simmons, who last played with the Los Angeles Clippers in April 2025, celebrated his Kings deal on social media on Saturday morning (AEST) by posting a photograph of himself wearing a team cap.

While reigniting Simmons's NBA career, his latest move is also a step towards possible Australian Boomers selection for next year's FIBA World Cup in Qatar and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

The Boomers, under Washington Wizards assistant and former NBL guard Adam Caporn, are chasing a podium return after a breakthrough bronze medal at the Tokyo Olympics five years ago.

Simmons spent his year out of basketball rebuilding his body and gathered momentum in his comeback bid during a Boomers mini-camp in Melbourne last month.

The former Philadelphia 76ers (2017-21), Brooklyn Nets (2022-25) and Clippers (2024-25) guard also reportedly attracted serious attention from the reigning champion New York Knicks and Golden State Warriors before he signed with Sacramento.

Simmons was drafted as the No.1 overall by Philadelphia in 2016, but missed his entire first season with a foot injury before establishing himself as one of the league's brightest young stars.

He claimed 2017-18 rookie ‌of the year honours and was a two-time All-Defensive ​pick before further injuries derailed his career.

Simmons has not played more than 58 games ​in ​a season since 2018-19.

He ​has averaged 13.1 points, ‌7.4 rebounds, 7.2 assists and 1.5 steals in 383 career games (344 starts) with the 76ers, Nets and Clippers.

Sacramento open the NBA preseason at home against the Los Angeles Lakers on October ​5, and visit the Clippers for their regular-season opener on ​October 21.

The Kings were 22-60 last season, finishing 14th in the Western Conference, and have only reached the playoffs once since 2006.

They suffered a first-round loss to Golden State in 2023, and have not won a playoff series since 2004.

AAP

World.title: Williams sisters knocked out by Aussie Joint and Chan
World.content:
Australian Maya Joint has again spoiled the part for the legendary Williams sisters, teaming up with Hao-Ching Chan to knock Serena and Venus out of the first round of the US Open women's doubles.

In front of a packed and passionate crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium, Joint and Chan came from 0-5 down in the deciding 10-point tiebreaker to down the legendary sisters 6-3, 6-7 (6/8), 7-6 (10/7).

This is the second consecutive grand slam that Joint has played spoiler, knocking Serena out in the first round of the Wimbledon ladies singles on Centre Court.

After losing the second set in a tiebreaker, Joint and Chan were in control of the third set with a 4-1 lead, before the Williams sisters fought back.

Serena Williams (right) of the United States and Venus Williams (left) of the United States in action against Hao-Ching Chan of Chinese Taipei and Maya Joint of Australia in the first round of doubles on Day 6 of the US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on September 04, 2026 in New York City (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Serena and Venus looked set for a dream comeback win when they held a huge 5-0 lead in the first to 10.

But both sisters double-faulted as Joint and Chan won 10 of the final 12 points to take the match.

The Williams sisters were supposed to make their grand slam doubles return at Wimbledon, but had to pull out after Serena hurt her knee.

That delayed their return to the Grand Slam stage until New York, where they won in 1999 and 2009 and are now 27-8 in their 10 appearances.

The match got a spot in the night session in Arthur Ashe Stadium — practically unheard of for first-round doubles.

The sisters were once dominant in women's doubles, teaming to win 14 grand slam titles along with Olympic gold medals in 2000, 2008 and 2012. They shared the number one ranking in women's doubles for eight weeks.

It appeared a first-round loss in 2022 was their last time together, with Serena stepping away from tennis that year after winning 23 Grand Slam singles titles. She came back this summer and now has two heartbreaking defeats with her older sister. They also lost in a match tiebreaker at the Cincinnati Open.

Venus Williams also lost in the first round of singles.

ABC/AP

World.title: That viral 'bulls***' moment and how football saved Awer Mabil
World.content:
Awer Mabil will never forget his first football, because he made it himself.

"We used to collect plastic bags and then tie them up into a ball shape," he tells triple j hack.

"It was pretty cool."

Loading...

Mabil is remembering his childhood in the Kakuma Refugee Camp where he was born in north-western Kenya.

"Football was 100 per cent an escape for us," he says.

"If you're hungry, you don't feel hungry because you're just playing for the moment with your friends.

"Then when I came to Australia, I was like, 'oh … I don't have to make the balls from the scratch.'"

Mabil and his family arrived in Australia as refugees when he was 10-years-old.

Since then he's established himself as one of Australia's most well-known football players, representing the nation at two World Cups, and being recognised as the Young Australian of the Year in 2023.

Awer Mabil has become one of Australia's most recognisable footballers and was named Young Australian of the Year in 2023. (AAP Image/Dave Hunt) (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Now 30, Mabil is back in Australia after a decade playing in Europe, achieving his dreams.

Earlier this year, the Socceroos star signed a three-year deal with Melbourne City and says he's looking forward to putting some roots down here.

"I can finally buy furniture that I can keep," he laughs.

" I also want to play in front of my family and friends ... I didn't take advantage of it when I was here before and now I get that chance again. "

'We're all proud'

Returning to Adelaide from the Socceroos World Cup campaign in July, Mabil made headlines when he was asked about One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's calls for a "monoculture" in Australia.

Loading TikTok content

"It's just all bulls***," Mabil told waiting reporters.

Now with a few months distance, the football player says he's still surprised by how much traction his response got.

"To be honest, it just came to my head," he tells hack.

"I was just being myself.

"I feel passionate about including everybody because that's what makes Australia great.

"So if there are people that try to divide what Australia is then that's not good."

Mabil says it's important to not only tolerate other cultures in Australia, but celebrate them.

"My little brothers were born here and they're more Aussie than anybody else.

"But everybody's got different flavours."

Mabil says many have thrown their support behind his defence of multiculturalism in recent months, but concedes there has been hate as well.

"I don't let that energy get to me."

"I've learned that being genuine, being pure to yourself and honest is best.

"Don't take in negativity."

Returning to Kakuma

One of Awer Mabil's biggest focuses in life, away from sport, is charity.

After a trip back to the camp where he was born, he and his brother started the charity Barefoot to Boots which supports refugees living in camps around the world by supplying them with football boots and equipment.

"It's very humbling," he says.

"Every time I go back it brings me back to appreciating the life that I have, that we have here in Australia, because people are struggling with the basic stuff there."

Non-government organisation Barefoot to Boots uses soccer to tackle global inequality and promote "health, education and gender equality initiatives" in refugee camps, especially at Kakuma in Kenya. Photo taken in 2018. (Facebook: Barefoot to Boots)

Barefoot to Boots has expanded its scope in recent years, funding sanitary products for girls, hospital equipment, teaching supplies and building public bathrooms.

"We went into the hospitals and realised the premature born kids didn't have a chance.

"So we donated three incubators and to be honest that's the best thing we've ever done because that's saving lives."

'Learn to love yourself'

Mabil says a bit of time has helped him better appreciate the Socceroos' effort at this year's World Cup, after the Australian team was beaten in a Round of 32 clash against Egypt.

It was just the third time the Socceroos had reached the knockout stage of the tournament.

"We were so close to making history," he says.

"We should be proud as a team.

"The future is looking great and I'm very optimistic about Australian football."

Socceroos star Awer Mabil isn't sure what will come after his football but says he will tackle whatever comes next with the same dedication as his playing career. (triple j hack: Arianna Lucente)

Asked what his future holds after football, Mabil smiles.

"It's an interesting question.

"I enjoy media a lot and could go down that path.

" But whatever I choose next … I'll put the same discipline into it that I did towards my football career. "

His advice for other young Australians who may be struggling with identity or feeling different is simple.

"Learn to love yourself.

"Remember … I'm created perfectly the way I am."

World.title: Clarkson opens up about 'publicly humilating' Kangaroos axing
World.content:
Alastair Clarkson says he and his family have been "publicly humiliated" by the way North Melbourne handled his sacking as head coach.

Clarkson has given his first interview since being let go by the Kangaroos on Wednesday.

Kangaroos president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney were brutally honest at their media conference in explaining why Clarkson was sacked with a year to go on his contract.

Clarkson, a four-time premiership coach at Hawthorn, said his family felt insulted by Hood and Viney's appearance in front of reporters.

"We're just shocked, and we just thought we were owed a little bit of respect in being informed and warned," Clarkson told The Age.

Alastair Clarkson leaves North North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

"Instead, they chose to dance on my grave like this."

Clarkson, who coached the Kangaroos for four seasons, added: "We all feel … so publicly humiliated."

He rejected suggestions his relationships with players and staff had deteriorated.

"Is that all my fault, is it?" Clarkson said.

"My mantra has never changed, and that has been to have care and empathy to help players chase their dream.

"I feel like my life's shot."

Premiership coaches John Longmire and Adam Simpson have been floated as options to take over from Clarkson, due to their stature as champion former Kangaroos players.

But after watching first-time coaches Steven King and Josh Fraser succeed this year, the Kangaroos could be inclined to find a highly rated assistant.

Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) were in contention for the Carlton job, before Fraser's results as interim coach made him the only choice for the Blues.

AAP

World.title: Aussie star Myers beats Olympic champions to win Diamond League Final
World.content:
Australia's Cameron Myers has recorded the most significant win of his young career by taking out the men's 1,500 metres at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Myers became only the eighth Australian to win a Diamond League Final title when he clocked a time of three minutes and 30.14 seconds at the King Baudouin Stadium.

The 20-year-old beat home a stacked field featuring the two most recent Olympic champions in the event, the USA's Cole Hocker and Norwegian Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

"I wouldn't say this victory comes as a surprise to me," Myers said after the race.

"It's more a relief to finally showcase what I've been building toward over the last couple of years.

"It feels surreal, even though I always believed I had it in me. But it's so different to actually do it and actually execute it when it matters.

"This is going to be a fun memory to look back on."

Cameron Myers (right) pipped Kenya's Phanuel Koech to claim victory. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton)

Myers timed his final sprint in the home straight to perfection, narrowly edging out Kenyan teenager Phanuel Koech (3:30.18) and American Ethan Strand (3:30.50).

Ingebrigtsen, who was the Tokyo Olympic gold medallist, posted a time of 3:30.52 to finish in fourth place, with Hocker seventh in 3:30.80.

Coached by Dick Telford, Myers is the best Australian prospect in the men's 1,500m since 1960 Olympic champion Herb Elliott.

The Brussels victory is the latest chapter in the Canberran's stellar season.

Myers set a national record of 3:28.00 in winning the 1,500m at the Paris Diamond League meet in June.

The time is the second-fastest run in the world this year.

Myers won the mile (3:46.06) at another Diamond League meet, Eugene's Prefontaine Classic, in July and finished second to Scottish world-record holder Josh Kerr in the same event at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

Less than a week ago, Myers triumphed in the 1,500m (3:30.96) at Berlin's prestigious ISTAF meet.

Kurtis Marschall finished third in the men's pole vault. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Among other Australian results in Brussels, Kurtis Marschall was third on countback in the men's pole vault.

Marschall and second-placed Sondre Guttormsen of Norway both cleared 5.82m, with Greece's Emmanouil Karalis winning with a meet record of 6.12m.

Sweden's Olympic and world champion, Mondo Duplantis, was a late withdrawal due to leg tightness.

Lachlan Kennedy ran under 10 seconds for the fifth time this season in the men's 100m, posting 9.99 to be fourth behind winner and reigning world champion, Jamaica's Oblique Seville (9.90).

Matthew Denny was also fourth in the men's discus with a best throw of 68.04m.

Slovenian Kristjan Čeh produced a meet record of 71.29m to claim victory.

Two-time Commonwealth Games champion Rose Davies also just missed the podium in the women's 5,000m, finishing fourth in 14:37.47 behind Ethiopian victor Freweyni Hailu (14:35.20).

Fellow Australians Georgia Griffith (14:38.69) and Linden Hall (14:40.62) were sixth and 10th respectively.

World.title: George Russell hits back for Mercedes in Monza practice
World.content:
Formula 1 title contender George Russell has hit back at early pacesetters Ferrari with the fastest lap of ​the day for Mercedes in Italian Grand Prix practice.

Russell surged to the top of the standings in second practice at the fast Monza circuit.

His lap ​of one minute and 22.559 seconds was ‌0.120 quicker than Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who was second in session two.

Russell served a notice of intent ahead of Sunday's race, which he needs to win to close the 59-point gap to championship-leading teammate Kimi Antonelli.

Leclerc had clocked a best time of 1:23.008, which was 0.173 quicker than Ferrari teammate Lewis Hamilton, in the first practice session.

"There's still some work ahead of us as our competitors look strong, but ⁠so far the feeling with the car was solid," Leclerc said.

Seven-time champion Hamilton was fifth in the second session.

Antonelli, who is set to start from the back of the grid due to engine penalties, was third fastest in the second session and 0.141 off the pace.

McLaren's reigning world champion, Lando Norris, was fourth, while his Australian teammate, Oscar Piastri, was sixth in the second session.

Norris has won the past two races and will be chasing a hat-trick on Sunday.

"The pace isn't where we need it to be right now," Norris said.

Gasly docked Monaco podium

Alpine's Pierre Gasly was stripped of his third place at the Monaco Grand Prix and Isack Hadjar reinstated to third position following a successful appeal by two Formula 1 teams.

Gasly dropped to seventh place in the June 7 race after ​a pair of ‌five-second penalties were applied.

Pierre Gasly was relegated to seventh place in the Monaco Grand Prix standings. (Getty Images/NurPhoto: Luca Rossini)

Initially, the penalties for speeding infractions had been rescinded one week after the race.

McLaren and Red Bull appealed to ‌the FIA's International Court of Appeal, with a hearing held ⁠in Paris on August 25.

The decision to ‌reinstate the original finish order ​was announced Friday.

Piastri was elevated to fourth place following the successful appeal.

Reuters

World.title: Opals make winning start to World Cup campaign
World.content:
Australia's women's basketball team have begun their World Cup campaign in Germany with an entertaining 70-54 win over Puerto Rico.

The Opals were pushed throughout by their opponents in the Group C opener in Berlin.

Steph Talbot was superb for Australia, earning the player-of-the-game award after posting 19 points, eight rebounds and three assists.

Ezi Magbegor also reached double figures in scoring with 11 points and led the way on the boards with nine.

Alanna Smith starred with 10 points and eight rebounds but left the court during the game with what looked like a lower left-leg injury.

Jade Melbourne chipped in with 10 points, while Zitina Aokuso and Isobel Borlaise had six each to help get the job done on day one of competition.

Arella Guirantes (14 points), Trinity San Antonio (11) and Imani McGee-Stafford (11) were Puerto Rico's top scorers.

Ranked third in the world behind the USA and France, the Opals were unbeaten in qualifying and crowned Asia Cup champions in 2025.

They have won medals in three of the past four World Cups since winning gold in Brazil 20 years ago.

They claimed silver in Spain in 2018, as well as bronze in Türkiye four years earlier and again on home soil in 2022.

The Opals face world number 16 Türkiye on Sunday and fifth-ranked Belgium the following day.

AAP

World.title: What are the World Nomad Games and why are Australians competing?
World.content:
The horse is already moving when Sezim Jumabekova draws her bow.

She has three targets to hit before the track runs out.

She grips the horse with her thighs, twists at the waist, and shoots.

Ms Jumabekova, 29, from Kyrgyzstan, has been riding competitively for only three years.

"I've fallen off many times and torn my clothes learning new tricks," she said.

Sezim Jumabekova tries out new tricks ahead of the opening ceremony. (Supplied: Sezim Jumabekova)

Despite being a relative newcomer to the sport, she is competing in horseback archery in the World Nomad Games from August 31 to September 6 in Kyrgyzstan.

Kyrgyzstan launched the World Nomad Games in 2014 as a stage for the traditional sports and cultures of Central Asia's nomadic peoples.

What began with 20 countries and 10 traditional sports has grown, in just over a decade, into an international competition of about 100 countries competing across 43 events.

Repackaging heritage as sport

An eagle hunter, also known as berkutchi, competes. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

Some of the sports are obscure outside the region, like eagle and falcon hunting and Kok-boru, where a horseback team wrestles for a sheep.

"It's like AFL and the NRL here in Australia, but on horseback," said Ahmed Kharat, captain of the Australian team competing in archery events in this year's games.

Many of the sports have cultural significance and local audiences.

Eagle hunting on command traces back to the Mongol conquests of the 12th and 13th centuries.

Falconry is a traditional sport with hunting assisted by Taigan hounds. (Reuters: Pavel Mikheyev)

Other events trace a long lineage.

An 11-kilometre horse race is among some of the equestrian events that have a rich history in neighbouring Mongolia and Kazakhstan.

Another is Er enish, a traditional Kyrgyz horseback wrestling sport.

The team from Kazakhstan unseated opponents to win gold in both the 60-kilogram and 70-kilogram categories this year.

Two teams compete in Kok-Boru, throwing a stuffed sheepskin into a goal for points. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

There are several other competitions competed on foot.

One times how quickly teams put up a yurt, a traditional portable nomadic dwelling used by nomadic families moving between pastures.

In another event called Ordo, teams use sheep knucklebones to flick opposing pieces from a marked ring.

Eagle hunting dates back to the Mongol Empire days. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

From Soviet torpedo factories to Insta-stan famous

The World Nomad Games is more than entertainment.

Regional commentators also point to their political and economic purpose.

Kyrgyzstan is a young state, which became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991, building its national identity from its nomadic past.

It was deeply integrated into the Soviet industrial machine, with one of its largest factories producing torpedoes for the Soviet navy.

The 6th World Nomad Games kicked off this week in Kyrgyzstan. (Reuters: Pavel Mikheyev)

When the Soviet Union collapsed, so did those jobs.

"Kyrgyzstan is quite unique as it experienced a lot of outward migration to the countryside after the collapse," said Kiril Nourzhanov, an associate professor in Central Asian Studies at the Australian National University.

"The economy of Kyrgyzstan was hit for six, and it experienced deindustrialisation, so more people began to engage in agriculture, including the traditional nomadic pastoralism," he added.

A service economy has emerged in the gap, and tourism now ranks among the country's most valuable sectors.

Tourism has soared in recent years, with tour companies such as Intrepid Travel reporting a 900 per cent increase in bookings to Kyrgyzstan this year compared to last year.

Delegates from Russia and Iran attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan this week. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

Gulshat Rozyyeva, a research scholar from the Australian National University's Centre for Arab and Islamic Studies, called the Games "a major identity booster".

She said it was an opportunity for Kyrgyzstan to appear as more than "one of Central Asia's poor countries".

"It doesn't have the natural resources like Kazakhstan or Turkmenistan," she said.

"But it has mountains, and a horse culture, and so the World Nomad Games are important economically, too, as people book hotels, and support local businesses."

Horse tricks were performed during the opening ceremony. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

The Kyrgyz government has invested heavily in that image: horses grazing on a backdrop of snow-capped mountains and pristine blue lakes.

This year the World Nomad Games double as a diplomatic stage, hosting delegates from Russia, Iran, India, and China at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan's capital, Bishkek.

Ms Rozyyeva said the balancing act was a familiar one for Kyrgyzstan — asserting a distinct national identity while leaning economically on its larger neighbours.

China invests in infrastructure in the country under the Belt and Road Initiative, while migrant workers in Russia send remittances back home to Kyrgyzstan.

A digital revival of an analogue culture

Ms Jumabekova grew up in Bishkek, far from the high mountain pastures traditionally associated with the country's nomadic culture.

She was teased for being a city girl, but was drawn to learning about horses and became a guide leading horseback tours, learning acrobatics and trick riding.

She said she was passionate about rediscovering skills from semi-nomadic life.

"Nowadays young people are interested in the digital world," she told the ABC.

"Each year it gets harder to save our nomad culture, perhaps because it brings in less money."

Participants from the UK take part in a tug-of-war competition. (Reuters:Pavel Mikheyev)

The irony is that the digital world and Instagram videos from tourists may also be helping preserve it.

Australian archer Daniya Aziz, 23, said that these sports haven't just seen a revitalisation in Central Asia.

"I think in the age that we are in, because we're so social media heavy, so technologically dependent, there has been … an urge to sort of disconnect from that," she said.

"There's no better way to do that than through these cultural sports because they have that element of physicality and an element of being outdoors.

Speed yurt assembly is one of the more traditional sports in the games. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

" It's a really nice way for us, from diverse backgrounds in Australia, to connect back to that culture identity. "

Ms Aziz said she was attracted to horseback archery for its challenge.

When contestants arrive in Kyrgyzstan, they pick sticks from a hat as part of a lottery and are allocated a horse at random.

"What's really cool about horseback archery is that it's building that connection between horse and archer so that when you are going down a track, you're going down as one unit," she said.

Kyrgyz archer Asel Sadyrova believes these sports also promote aspirations for girls today, building strength and confidence while keeping alive history that may otherwise be forgotten.

Asel Sadyrova is teaching girls in Kyrgyzstan traditional wooden bow archery. (Supplied: Asel Sadyrova)

"Epics and tales passed down preserve our nation, and my grandfather's stories about heroic, courageous women who defend their people from enemies make me remember we are the heroines of the modern age," she said.

"I believe young people want to follow in the footsteps of these heroines."

Tech.title: Audacity 4 is a complete revamp of the ‘world’s most popular’ audio editor
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn’t nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more importantly, all the promised improvements to the self-proclaimed “world’s most popular audio editing and recording app” are here, turning Audacity from a free and capable but extremely clunky audio editor into a powerful modern tool.

The biggest change is the move to a non-destructive editing workflow. That means you can trim a clip down, then recover the audio simply by dragging the edge of the clip back out if you change your mind. Clips can now overlap too, which means you can still paste in audio even if there isn’t enough space and adjust after, or just freely drag audio around the timeline. Previously, if you tried to drag a clip past another one in the timeline, it would just stop dead in its tracks. You’d instead have to cut and paste it to move it past any existing audio.

You can also split clips now to easily chop up and rearrange audio. The developers refreshed clip envelopes and the built-in effects, and added a home screen with revamped project organization. Audacity also got a dramatic facelift that brings it more in line with Muse’s other products like Muse Score and Audio.com, complete with customizable themes.

While Audacity has been a staple of many people’s toolkits since it debuted way back in 2000, it’s stayed stubbornly consistent in its design and layout as new features have been bolted on, sometimes clumsily. This big refresh to Audacity 4 brings it much closer to a modern digital audio workstation (DAW).

Tech.title: The White House is making arcade games racist
Tech.content:
is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed “arcade” games, some of which are racist — and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be associated with the MAGA agenda.

The Tetris Company has already responded to “Build the Wall,” which is obviously modeled on the famous puzzle game. In the Trump administration’s game, the player has to stack interlocking shapes to stop a “zombie border siege” along the southern border. Aliens — the administration’s preferred term for noncitizens, and the subject of previous grotesque attempts at humor — run across the screen, trying to get to America before the gates are shut.

In a statement to The Verge, Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca clarified that the company wasn’t involved in the creation of Donald Trump’s game. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy. The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible,” Brusca said. “We are currently reviewing the matter.”

The various companies whose brands the White House ripped off to make and promote these games — including Sega, Nintendo, Xbox, and the Flappy Bird Foundation Group — did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Previously, the Trump administration has gotten in trouble for infringing on others’ copyrights. The Department of Homeland Security has had to delete some of its racist, fancam-esque posts after receiving DMCA takedown requests.

The purpose of Trump’s interminable memes, games, and other gimmicks is manifold: to drum up support for Trump’s policies, to entertain his groyper fans, and, of course, to troll the libs. (One game, “Rio Run,” is like snake, except the head of the snake is a Border Patrol agent who collects migrants as he moves across the screen. Ha ha, get it? The president is deporting people.) But the games also inadvertently highlight the administration’s policy failures, not to mention the hypocrisy of Trump’s agenda.

Trump’s efforts to build a wall through protected lands in the Southwest, including Big Bend National Park, has been met with mass opposition — even from Republicans in deep-red Texas who form a key part of the MAGA coalition.

Other games are similar reminders of how Trump’s policies are backfiring, even on the right.

There’s “Flappy Bill,” a play on Flappy Bird that involves getting a bald eagle to deliver a piece of legislation to the National Mall. Cute! Except the administration has rolled back protections under the Endangered Species Act, the landmark legislation that helped rescue bald eagles from the brink of extinction. The administration’s supposed revamping of the National Mall has also been unpopular.

In “Supply Line,” reminiscent of the game Tapper, you have to knock processed foods — those filled with additives, seed oils, and artificial colorings — off a conveyor belt before they get fed to schoolchildren. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hasn’t managed to do any of that. Besides issuing a likely AI-drafted report for his Make America Healthy Again commission, RFK Jr.’s main role at HHS has been to roll back vaccine recommendations and food safety regulations. The administration’s gutting of the Food and Drug Administration made it harder to investigate the spread of cyclosporiasis, the so-called explosive diarrhea parasite, earlier this year.

If anything, these games serve as a great reminder that our well-being is a big joke to the president and the people who surround him.

Tech.title: GoPro says it’s still committed ‘to your collective stoke’
Tech.content:
To our GoPro community, fans and customers,

We understand there’s some concern about GoPro’s post-merger commitment to continue developing market leading cameras for consumers and professionals. Making amazing cameras for all of you is our core DNA and reason for being and that will never change! We’re fired up about what’s ahead for GoPro and want to share a little more about what our proposed merger with Starman means for our future.

Thanks to the improved financial strength this merger will provide, we’ll be in a much better position to innovate, invent and advance the future of consumer and professional content creation. And importantly, Starman shares our passion for the GoPro brand, developing market leading products and our commitment to your collective stoke.

We’ve accumulated more than 2500 patents over the last 24 years which tells you we’ve been busy innovating, and this merger will ensure we’re able to innovate for many more years to come. We expect this merger will make GoPro a stronger, more capable camera company than ever before.

Our goal is to become a more diversified company which can make us stronger financially, enabling GoPro to become as awesome as we (and you) want us to be. We plan to bring you more innovative cameras, smarter accessories, and more powerful software and services designed to make capturing, editing and sharing your experiences easier and more exciting than ever. We see opportunities to improve the products you already love while developing new tools and experiences that help you create, connect and share in entirely new ways.

We have so much more to do, so much more to invent, and so much more we want to bring to the GoPro community. We appreciate all of you who have been on this journey with us and we’re excited about where we’re headed. We’re going to keep doing what we do best - making the world’s highest-performance cameras and building the products, services and innovations that help you capture life’s most exciting moments. It’s what we were founded to do and it’s what we will always do. Be a HERO…GoPro.

With respect and appreciation — Nick

GoPro Founder & CEO

Tech.title: Roland is getting into generative AI music with Melody Flip
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

It’s not quite the “push button; get song” of Suno, but Roland’s new Melody Flip tool marks the company’s foray into generative AI music. Available as a plug-in for your digital audio workstation (DAW), Melody Flip offers around 250 “Palettes,” which are essentially themed collections of musical ideas sorted by genre. You can start from scratch and ask it to generate any combination of melody, chord progression, bassline, or drums. Or you can feed it a reference track and have it build off the melodic ideas from that.

Unlike Suno or Udio, Melody Flip doesn’t spit out fully polished songs with vocals and full arrangements. Instead, it offers simple musical loops meant to serve as a creative spark for you to build on. There are fairly limited control over the outputs. You can’t feed Melody Flip a text prompt like “acoustic country rock with clean male vocals, literate singer-songwriter, gentle brushed drums, and sparse pedal steel at 98BPM” and get a Jason Isbell ripoff. Instead, you basically just choose a genre, note density, BPM, musical key, and take what you get. Though the genre options are pretty fine-grained, going from standard fare like “80s disco” and “90s R&B” to esoteric things like “Kawaii Future Bass” and “Anime World.”

The sound selection is further proof that you’re not supposed to use Melody Flip outputs out of the box. The presets available are mostly the sort of general MIDI tones you’d find in ‘90s video games. It seems like the intended use is to export the MIDI data from Melody Flip directly into your DAW to manipulate and pair with other, more powerful synth plugins.
